theft-and-robbery/returning-a-stolen-ite.description: May a thief return a stolen item that is now worthless, like old coins or an expired ticket? Rav Yehuda and Rav Huna argue, in Bava Kamma 96.

theft-and-robbery/returning-stolen-items.intro: A thief who repents must give back what he took, but what if the owner has already despaired of ever seeing it again? Bava Kamma 67b records a debate that lasted decades: Rabba says the thief may pay money instead, while Rav Yosef insists the item itself must go back. In the end, the halacha follows Rav Yosef.
theft-and-robbery/returning-stolen-items.description: Must a repentant thief return the stolen item itself once the owner has given up hope? Rabba and Rav Yosef debate yiush for decades in Bava Kamma 67b.

theft-and-robbery/spiking-food-to-stop-a.intro: Where beis din has authority, would it stop someone from adding a laxative to his own labeled milk in a shared fridge to catch a food thief? Based on Bava Kamma 47a, the Derech Emunah says beis din would not step in, since only a thief is affected, while the Maharsham may disagree. One man simply wrote on his milk that a laxative was added, and it was never touched again.
theft-and-robbery/spiking-food-to-stop-a.description: May you spike your own food in a shared fridge to stop a thief? The Derech Emunah and Maharsham on whether beis din steps in, from Bava Kamma 47a.

theft-and-robbery/stealing-to-save-a-lif.intro: Kesubos 19a teaches that nothing stands in the way of saving a life except murder, idolatry and arayos, and the Shulchan Aruch rules one may steal to save a life. But must the rescuer pay back? Chazal exempted a rescuer from damages he causes, yet Rav Moshe Feinstein says that enactment does not cover theft, which must still be repaid.
theft-and-robbery/stealing-to-save-a-lif.description: May you steal to save a life, and must you pay it back afterward? Kesubos 19a, the Shulchan Aruch and Rav Moshe Feinstein on restitution after a rescue.

lost-objects/keeping-unclaimed-lost-item.intro: What if the owner of a lost item never comes back for it? Rav Asher Weiss says the finder may write down its value and then keep or sell it, paying the owner if he ever returns, and this works for most items, like toys and coats, but not a rare sefer or special tefillin. The discussion builds on the switched utensils of Bava Basra 46a.
lost-objects/keeping-unclaimed-lost-item.description: May a finder record an unclaimed item's value and then use or sell it? Rav Asher Weiss says yes for most items, in a discussion built on Bava Basra 46a.

lost-objects/mixed-up-laundry-or-dry-cle.intro: If the dry cleaner hands you someone else's pants, may you wear them, or hold on to them until yours turn up? The Terumas HaDeshen says no to both. [Lost in the Shuffle](/daf/bava-basra/46/lost-in-the-shuffle) explains that his ruling rests on Bava Basra 46a, where a utensil switched at a wedding or a house of mourning may not be used without permission.
lost-objects/mixed-up-laundry-or-dry-cle.description: May you wear the wrong garment the cleaner gave you, or keep it until yours is found? The Terumas HaDeshen says no, based on Bava Basra 46a.

lost-objects/taking-the-wrong-coat.intro: You leave shul in the rain and find your coat gone, with a similar one left on the rack. Bava Basra 46a makes clear that you may not use it just because its owner took yours. Modern poskim note some leniencies, and Rav Moshe Feinstein suggested that every shul post a sign granting permission in advance.
lost-objects/taking-the-wrong-coat.description: Someone took your coat at shul. May you wear the one left behind? Bava Basra 46a says no, but poskim add leniencies, and Rav Moshe suggested a sign.

business-ethics/ani-mehapech-bacharara.intro: If someone is already working to get a job or an item, another person who snatches it first is called a rasha. Rashi applies this widely, while Tosfos say a bargain or ownerless item is open to all. [A Grab Bag Of Halachos](/daf/bava-basra/145/a-grab-bag-of-halachos) adds Rav Elchanan's point from Bava Basra 145 that the rule needs effort by the first person, so it does not cover a free gift.
business-ethics/ani-mehapech-bacharara.description: When is it wrong to grab a deal another is pursuing? Rashi and Tosfos on ani mehapech bacharara, and Rav Elchanan's view on gifts, from Bava Basra 145.

business-ethics/boycotting-price-gouging.intro: When gentile merchants drove up the price of fish for Shabbos, some wanted a boycott, while others said money spent on Shabbos is always repaid. The Tzemach Tzedek ruled for the boycott, since the poor could not lay out the money now, and oneg Shabbos can be fulfilled with other foods. [Something Fishy](/daf/taanis/15/something-fishy) connects his ruling to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's stand on bird prices in Bava Basra 96a.
business-ethics/boycotting-price-gouging.description: May a community boycott Shabbos fish to fight price gouging? The Tzemach Tzedek's ruling and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's bird prices, Bava Basra 96a.

business-ethics/kofin-al-middas-sedom.intro: Kofin al middas Sedom means a person can be forced not to act like the selfish people of Sedom, when helping costs him nothing. On a sinking ship, may one passenger force another to throw his cheap copper overboard to save his gold? Discussing Bava Kamma 116b, Tosfos says the rule works only after the fact, while the Rema and Aruch HaShulchan allow more.
business-ethics/kofin-al-middas-sedom.description: Can you force someone not to act selfishly when helping costs him nothing? Tosfos and the Rema on kofin al middas Sedom, in a case from Bava Kamma 116b.

business-ethics/meddling-in-other-people.intro: Someone who helps one person at another's expense in a matter that does not concern him is called a rasha arum, a cunning wicked person. So how could Abaye suggest a plan that would make Moshe ben Itzri pay? [A Matter of Opinion](/daf/bava-basra/174/a-matter-of-opinion) explains the Gemara's answer on Bava Basra 174b: the father should have been supporting his son, a Torah scholar.
business-ethics/meddling-in-other-people.description: Is it wrong to help one person at another's expense when it isn't your business? The rasha arum warning and Abaye's exception, from Bava Basra 174b.

business-ethics/opening-a-competing-scho.intro: Normally one may not encroach on another person's livelihood, but may a new yeshiva open where one already exists? [Schooled On The Competition](/daf/bava-basra/21/schooled-on-the-competition) shows from Bava Basra 21 that Torah teaching is different, because competition makes schools better. The Chazon Ish even says that blocking a new school is like shedding blood.
business-ethics/opening-a-competing-scho.description: May a new yeshiva open in a neighborhood that already has one? Bava Basra 21 encourages competition in Torah teaching, and the Chazon Ish defends it.

business-ethics/rabbinic-copyright-on-se.intro: The Shapira family spent heavily on a new Slavuta Shas, so rabbanim signed letters forbidding anyone else to print one for a fixed time. When the Romm brothers began a rival edition in 1834, they argued that the period had run out. Rebbe Akiva Eiger, who had signed the original ban, agreed that it had expired, in an article on Beitzah 37.
business-ethics/rabbinic-copyright-on-se.description: Why did rabbis forbid printing a rival Shas for a set time? The Slavuta ban and Rebbe Akiva Eiger's ruling that it had ended, in an article on Beitzah 37.

business-ethics/recommending-a-cheaper-s.intro: May you tell others that one Jewish store is cheaper than another? HaRav Hillel Zaks says no, comparing it to the warning on Bava Basra 174b against getting involved in matters that are not yours, and he forbids posting it in a group chat. HaRav Nissin Karelitz disagrees, and the poskim and publications cited take differing positions.
business-ethics/recommending-a-cheaper-s.description: May you post in a group chat that one store is cheaper? HaRav Hillel Zaks forbids it, based on Bava Basra 174b, and HaRav Nissin Karelitz permits it.

business-ethics/recruiting-students-from.intro: A new school may open next to an old one, but may it go after children already enrolled elsewhere? Tosfos and the Igros Moshe say a rebbi may not offer himself to replace another, though parents may choose to switch on their own. Discussing Bava Basra 21, the article rejects the claim that a school that thinks it is better may recruit.
business-ethics/recruiting-students-from.description: May a yeshiva actively recruit students from another school? Tosfos and the Igros Moshe say no, even if it feels superior. A discussion from Bava Basra 21.

business-ethics/saving-a-seat-for-someon.intro: Boruch is stuck at the back of a crowded bus stop, so he calls his chavrusa Shimon, already on the bus, to save him a seat. In [Can You Save Me a Seat?](/daf/gittin/11/can-you-save-me-a-seat), based on Gittin 11b, the two trade sources on seizing assets for creditors. Rav Zilberstein's comparison to a family member saving seats for his own family offers the best way through.
business-ethics/saving-a-seat-for-someon.description: May you save a bus seat for a friend while others must stand? A playful debate built on the laws of seizing assets for a creditor in Gittin 11b.

business-ethics/selling-non-kosher-food-.intro: Pesachim 23a teaches that hunters who catch non-kosher species by accident may sell them to gentiles, but may not trap them on purpose to trade. The Gilyon Tosfos, as explained by the Pnei Yehoshua, holds this ban is only rabbinic, out of concern that the seller may come to eat. Rav Moshe Sternbuch urged a ba'al teshuvah to leave such a business, while the Ksav Sofer found room to be lenient for an innkeeper.
business-ethics/selling-non-kosher-food-.description: May a Jew make or sell non-kosher food for gentile customers? Pesachim 23a, the Pnei Yehoshua, Rav Moshe Sternbuch and the Ksav Sofer weigh in.

business-ethics/selling-the-wrong-produc.intro: A shopkeeper sold salt instead of sugar, and a whole Kiddush of desserts was ruined, and the customer wants him to pay. [Sweet and Salty](/daf/bava-kamma/35/sweet-and-salty), filed on Bava Kamma 35, weighs whether this is indirect damage, a pit, or a fire carried by the wind. The posek finally suggests a settlement.
business-ethics/selling-the-wrong-produc.description: A shopkeeper sold salt instead of sugar and ruined a customer's desserts. Must he pay? A case of grama, pit and fire, filed on Bava Kamma 35.

business-ethics/teaching-about-business-.intro: Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai spent forty years in business and knew every trick of dishonest dealers. Should he teach them so honest people avoid mistakes, even though cheats might learn new tricks? [In All Honesty](/daf/bava-basra/89/in-all-honesty) explains the Gemara on Bava Basra 89a, the Maharsha's question, and why in the end he gave the shiur.
business-ethics/teaching-about-business-.description: Should you teach how cheats operate, if cheaters might learn from it? Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakai's dilemma about a shiur on business fraud, Bava Basra 89a.

business-ethics/tenant-farmer-and-crop-d.intro: The mishnah on Bava Metzia 105b lets a tenant farmer deduct from his rent when a general calamity, like strong winds or locusts, ruins his field; Rav Yehudah says most fields in the valley must be struck. But if the owner stipulated wheat and the tenant planted barley, he gets no deduction. The owner can argue that his Rosh Hashanah prayers for wheat might have spared the field, as [Like Father, Like Son](/daf/arachin/16/like-father-like-son) explains.
business-ethics/tenant-farmer-and-crop-d.description: May a tenant farmer cut his rent after locusts or wind ruin the crop? The mishnah on Bava Metzia 105b, and why planting barley instead of wheat matters.

workers-and-employers/a-workers-right-to.intro: Bava Metzia 10a teaches that a day laborer may quit in the middle of the day without penalty. The source is the verse that Bnei Yisrael are servants of Hashem, not servants to other servants. The Ritva calls it a scriptural decree: a worker may back out of a set term without losing the pay he already earned.
workers-and-employers/a-workers-right-to.description: May a hired worker quit in the middle of a job? Jews are servants of Hashem, not of people, so a day laborer can back out, as taught in Bava Metzia 10a.

workers-and-employers/changing-an-employ.intro: A worker hired for varied hours, including a night shift that ended at 3:30 in the morning, was later told to take the early shift starting at that hour instead, and refused. Rav Zilberstein rules that this is no grounds for dismissal. [Rise and Shine](/daf/yoma/21/rise-and-shine) explains his source on Yoma 21a: it is human nature to find waking early harder than staying up late, so the early shift goes beyond what the worker agreed to.
workers-and-employers/changing-an-employ.description: May an employer move a night worker to an early morning shift, or fire him for refusing? Rav Zilberstein's ruling based on Yoma 21a on waking early.

workers-and-employers/employers-responsi.intro: A merchant sent his agent on a business trip, and the agent was murdered on the way. The Be'er Sheva, learning from Dovid HaMelech and the city of Nov in Sanhedrin 95a, told the merchant to fast forty days and support the family. The Noda B'Yehudah says it is different when the traveler came up with the trip himself.
workers-and-employers/employers-responsi.description: Is a merchant responsible if the agent he sent on a trip is killed? The Be'er Sheva, Tzemach Tzedek and Noda B'Yehudah weigh Sanhedrin 95a and Nov.

workers-and-employers/forgiving-negligen.intro: Rabbah Bar Bar Chana's workers broke his barrels of wine, and he took their cloaks as payment. On Bava Metzia 83a, Rav told him to give them back, citing the verse about following the road of the good. Rashi explains that the workers were negligent but did not mean it, so Rabbah should go beyond the letter of the law.
workers-and-employers/forgiving-negligen.description: Should you forgive workers who caused a loss by mistake? Rav told Rabbah Bar Bar Chana to return their cloaks, going beyond the law, in Bava Metzia 83a.

workers-and-employers/paying-wages-for-f.intro: After the barrels broke, the poor workers told Rav they were hungry, and he told Rabbah to pay their wages too. In [A Cut Above](/daf/bava-metzia/83/a-cut-above), the Vilna Gaon explains that forgiving a debt is the road of the good, while paying money not owed is the rarer path of the righteous. The Chida says a sage like Rabbah was expected to act this way, based on Bava Metzia 83a.
workers-and-employers/paying-wages-for-f.description: Should an employer pay poor workers whose job ended in loss? Rav told Rabbah to pay, and the Vilna Gaon and Chida explain why, in Bava Metzia 83a.

workers-and-employers/paying-workers-at-.intro: The Gemara in Shevuos 45a says day laborers do not want to be paid at the start of the day. Rashi explains that they need the money for the household shopping at night and fear they will spend it on something else first. The Rashash reads Rashi as worried about losing the money, and the article finds an ancient example of impulse buying.
workers-and-employers/paying-workers-at-.description: Why did day laborers prefer to be paid in the evening? Rashi and the Rashash explain the Gemara in Shevuos 45a, which touches on impulse spending.

workers-and-employers/sick-pay-in-halach.intro: Must a school pay a rebbe who misses weeks of teaching because he is sick? Tosfos on Kiddushin 17a compare him to a day laborer, who is paid only for the hours he works, while the Maharam Mi'Rottenberg says whoever holds the money keeps it. [The Price to Pay](/daf/kiddushin/17/the-price-to-pay) concludes that in practice the employer's rules, or local custom, decide.
workers-and-employers/sick-pay-in-halach.description: Must an employer pay a teacher or worker for sick days? Tosfos, the Maharam and the Shach, with the role of contracts and custom, from Kiddushin 17a.

workers-and-employers/work-contracts-lon.intro: The Hagahos Mordechai warns that a work contract of more than three years can make a person like an eved, and the Rema rules this way. The Chasam Sofer applies it even to community rabbis, but Tosfos holds that anyone who may back out can sign for as long as he wants. The discussion grows out of Bava Metzia 10a.
workers-and-employers/work-contracts-lon.description: Can a long-term work contract make you like a servant? The Hagahos Mordechai, Chasam Sofer and Tosfos weigh three-year terms, from Bava Metzia 10a.

workers-and-employers/workers-oath-to-co.intro: On a busy payday, an employer may lose track of who was paid. Shevuos 45a lets the worker swear and collect on that day, but the next day the employer is believed. Tosfos asks why not just wait for the employer to remember, and answers that once he has claimed he paid, he will hold on to that belief.
workers-and-employers/workers-oath-to-co.description: When may a worker swear and collect pay his employer says he already gave? Shevuos 45a, Tosfos and why the timing of the claim matters so much.

buying-and-selling/acquiring-a-trapped-a.intro: The Mishnah in Gittin 59b teaches that animals caught in traps are not acquired until the trapper takes them, yet taking them is robbery because of the ways of peace. Rebbe Yosei says it is full robbery, but the halacha follows the Sages. If the trap truly holds the animal, like a cage, the trapper owns it outright, unlike a hook or leg snare.
buying-and-selling/acquiring-a-trapped-a.description: Does a trapper own an animal caught in his trap? The Mishnah in Gittin 59b, Rebbe Yosei and the Sages on cages, snares and the ways of peace.

buying-and-selling/agreements-made-under.intro: Tavi hung Pafi in a tree until he agreed to sell his harp. Rav Huna rules on Bava Basra 48 that the sale is valid, because in the end Pafi agreed once he was paid, though a forced gift would not be. [Harping on Divided Real Estate](/daf/bava-basra/48/harping-on-divided-real-estate) asks what someone facing such pressure can do to protect himself.
buying-and-selling/agreements-made-under.description: Is a sale made under pressure binding? Rav Huna upholds a forced sale once payment is received, but not a forced gift. The case is in Bava Basra 48.

buying-and-selling/chinese-auction-halac.intro: At a Chinese auction, some tickets fell out of the drum on the way to the podium, so the director stopped the drawing and redrew from the full pool. The Chavas Yair, citing Bava Basra 106b, ruled that a raffle missing one entry, or with a name entered twice, is entirely invalid and must be redone. [A Winning Ticket](/daf/bava-basra/106/a-winning-ticket) explains why many organizations print a disclaimer that no drawing will be repeated.
buying-and-selling/chinese-auction-halac.description: What happens when a Chinese auction drawing misses a ticket or counts one twice? The Chavas Yair's ruling from Bava Basra 106b and why disclaimers help.

buying-and-selling/easements-and-access-.intro: If a buyer forgets to write access rights into his contract, must he pay to walk through the seller's land? The Chachamim on Bava Basra 64a say he must, but Rebbe Akiva says access is automatically included, and the halacha follows him. [Simcha On The Side](/daf/bava-basra/64/simcha-on-the-side) applies this to a simcha hall sold by a yeshiva.
buying-and-selling/easements-and-access-.description: Does a buyer automatically get the right to cross the seller's land to reach what he bought? The Chachamim and Rebbe Akiva disagree in Bava Basra 64a.

buying-and-selling/kinyan-chalipin-with-.intro: At a wedding, the rabbi hands the chosson a pen, and with that kinyan chalipin the chosson takes on the kesubah. The same exchange is used to sell chametz. The item must be a utensil, so grapes will not do, but Tosfos on Bava Metzia 46b says even a cow works, because animals have designated uses like plowing.
buying-and-selling/kinyan-chalipin-with-.description: Why does a rabbi hand over a pen at a wedding or chametz sale? Kinyan chalipin needs a utensil, and Tosfos says even a cow can work, Bava Metzia 46b.

buying-and-selling/kinyan-meshichah-on-a.intro: One can acquire an animal through meshichah without pulling it, simply by calling it so it moves toward the caller. Tosfos in Kiddushin 26a adds that holding food above an animal so it jumps counts as lifting it. The Ketzos HaChoshen argues that baiting a hook so a fish swims toward it acquires the fish, as the article on Gittin 59b explains.
buying-and-selling/kinyan-meshichah-on-a.description: Can you acquire an animal by calling it or luring it with food? Tosfos in Kiddushin 26a and the Ketzos on a baited hook, in an article on Gittin 59b.

buying-and-selling/matanah-al-menas-leha.intro: Rava in Kiddushin 6b teaches that a gift given on condition it be returned is a real gift. This lets a neighbor use someone else's lulav and esrog on the first day of Sukkos, or a guest make a bracha on a borrowed tallis. But [Of Giving and Receiving](/daf/kiddushin/6/of-giving-and-receiving) shows that the same trick fails for mishloach manos, which must build friendship.
buying-and-selling/matanah-al-menas-leha.description: A gift given on condition it be returned lets one own a lulav or tallis for a mitzvah. Rava's rule in Kiddushin 6b, and where it does not work.

buying-and-selling/packages-left-on-a-do.intro: Does a homeowner own a gift left on his open doorstep? Bava Metzia 11a records a dispute about acquiring gifts in an unguarded chatzer: the Rambam and Shulchan Aruch say no, while Tosfos follows Rav Pappa. The Rema says the giver guards the spot for a moment, and the Aruch HaShulchan suggests a delivery driver or a fenced yard may do the same.
buying-and-selling/packages-left-on-a-do.description: Do you own a package left on an unguarded doorstep? The Rambam, Tosfos and the Rema debate acquiring gifts this way, based on Bava Metzia 11a.

buying-and-selling/renovated-house-as-a-.intro: A seller promised to provide a new house, then delivered an old one that was completely renovated. Has he kept his word? The Toras Chayim ties this to a dispute in Eruvin 53 about the new king over Egypt: if an old king with new decrees counts as new, then a fully redone house may count as new too.
buying-and-selling/renovated-house-as-a-.description: Does a fully renovated old house meet a contract for a new house? The Toras Chayim links it to the dispute over the new king of Egypt in Eruvin 53.

buying-and-selling/three-year-chazakah-o.intro: Someone who works a field quietly for three years is presumed to be its owner, unless shown otherwise. The original owner can stop this by protesting in public, since news spreads and the occupant will know to keep his documents. On Bava Basra 39b, the Gemara asks whether such a protest needs two people present or three.
buying-and-selling/three-year-chazakah-o.description: How does working land for three years make you its presumed owner, and how can a protest stop it? The chazakah rules of Bava Basra 39b, simply explained.

buying-and-selling/transactions-that-tak.intro: May a sale made before Shabbos be set to take effect on Shabbos itself? Rebbe Akiva Eiger, discussing the Kohen Gadol's marriage on Yoma 13b, concludes that completing a transaction on Shabbos is forbidden even with no action that day. The Terumas HaDeshen holds that such a transaction escapes the rabbinic decree, and the Mishnah Berurah follows his view.
buying-and-selling/transactions-that-tak.description: May a sale arranged before Shabbos take effect on Shabbos? Rebbe Akiva Eiger and the Terumas HaDeshen disagree, with the Mishnah Berurah. Yoma 13b.

buying-and-selling/what-a-house-sale-inc.intro: When someone sells a house without spelling out what is included, does a nearby small structure come with it? The Mishna on Bava Basra 61a says it does not, and Mar Zutra adds that this applies only if it is at least sixteen square amos. He leaves unclear whether an adjoining storage room needs that size too, a question the Maharam Shik ties to mezuzah.
buying-and-selling/what-a-house-sale-inc.description: If a house is sold with no details, are nearby structures or attached rooms included? The Mishna and Mar Zutra in Bava Basra 61a on size and significance.

neighbors/choosing-between-access-routes.intro: A yeshiva sold its simcha hall, then told the buyers to use the side door, not the main entrance. The Rema rules that a buyer cannot demand a specific route when another one is available. But the Nachal Yitzchak says that if one path is longer and crooked, the buyer may demand the shorter one, and the case on Bava Basra 64 is left for the poskim to decide.
neighbors/choosing-between-access-routes.description: Can a buyer insist on the nicer main entrance when a side door exists? The Rema and Nachal Yitzchak on choosing access routes, tied to Bava Basra 64.

neighbors/dissolving-a-business-partners.intro: Two families shared a successful real estate venture, but the title was in only one family's name. When they disagreed, that family offered to split it at a low value and threatened years in secular court. Building on Bava Basra 48, the Bais HaVaad case shows how the other family agreed under protest and later had the unfair division undone in beis din.
neighbors/dissolving-a-business-partners.description: One partner held the title and forced an unfair split of a joint real estate venture. How beis din undid it, in a case built on Bava Basra 48.

neighbors/lost-right-of-way-to-a-field.intro: A farmer returns from abroad to find the path to his landlocked field overgrown, and cannot remember which side it ran on. Yevamos 37b rules that if different neighbors own the surrounding fields, each can send him to the next, and even one buyer of all four need not provide a path. In [Flyover Country](/daf/yevamos/37/flyover-country), the Nesivos HaMishpat explains that this applies only to a right of use, not to a strip of land the farmer actually owned.
neighbors/lost-right-of-way-to-a-field.description: What if a farmer forgets where his path to a landlocked field ran? Yevamos 37b, the four neighbors, and the Nesivos HaMishpat on owning the path.

neighbors/public-use-of-private-property.intro: Bus riders have long sat on a homeowner's low brick wall; may he now build it higher and take away their seat? Rav Yehuda on Bava Basra 100a says a path the public has taken over may not be ruined, but the Rashbam requires that the public fixed it up, so Rav Zilberstein lets the owner build. Other rishonim disagree, and Rav Zilberstein adds a Maharsham: with recorded deeds today, the owner's silence proves no lasting consent.
neighbors/public-use-of-private-property.description: Can a homeowner take back a low wall that bus riders use as a bench? Rav Yehuda's rule on Bava Basra 100a, the Rashbam, and Rav Zilberstein's ruling.

neighbors/taking-the-law-into-your-own-h.intro: If a neighbor's animals keep grazing on your land despite repeated warnings, may you spread poison on your own property to stop them? The Derech Emunah says beis din will not interfere with what a person does on his own land. The Maharsham strongly disagrees, since one may not take the law into his own hands when he can go to beis din, as the article filed on Bava Kamma 56 explains.
neighbors/taking-the-law-into-your-own-h.description: Can you put poison on your land against a neighbor's trespassing animals? The Derech Emunah allows it; the Maharsham says go to beis din. Bava Kamma 56.

neighbors/using-a-neighbors-well-water.intro: During a drought, may you siphon water from a neighbor's private well without asking? Yehoshua made water sources on private land open to everyone, but Tosfos limits his rule to a spring, not a man-made well, and elsewhere says one may not trespass to reach even a public spring. [Water Works](/daf/avodah-zarah/59/water-works) works through Tosfos on Avodah Zarah 59a and ends with clear advice: dig your own well instead.
neighbors/using-a-neighbors-well-water.description: May you take water from a neighbor's private well during a drought? Yehoshua's rule, and why Tosfos on Avodah Zarah 59a turns off the tap for wells.

inheritance/deathbed-gift-to-one-sibling.intro: On her deathbed, the sister of Rav Tovi gave him all her property. His brother Rav Achadvoi complained that people would say only Rav Tovi was a real scholar, so she gave everything to Rav Achadvoi instead. Rav Elchanan Wasserman asks on Bava Basra 145 how that could be fair, and Rav Yaakov Emden explains that the request was really to split the gift between them.
inheritance/deathbed-gift-to-one-sibling.description: A dying sister gave everything to one brother, then to the other. Was that fair to the first? Rav Elchanan and Rav Yaakov Emden on Bava Basra 145 explain.

inheritance/dividing-an-inheritance-by-l.intro: Two brothers split their father's property by lottery, and then a long-lost third brother appeared. One brother, happy with his share, appeased the newcomer, but the other demanded a new lottery even though he lost nothing. The Gemara on Bava Basra 106b and the Shulchan Aruch rule that since the lottery was not done properly, any participant can demand that it be repeated.
inheritance/dividing-an-inheritance-by-l.description: Brothers split an inheritance by lottery, then a missing brother appears. May any heir demand a new drawing? The Gemara on Bava Basra 106b says yes.

inheritance/gift-given-for-a-specific-ne.intro: A father left his youngest son a valuable Russian army exemption card, but the son failed the physical and wanted to sell the card himself. His brothers asked the Rogatchover Gaon, who cited Nazir 24a: a husband gave his wife an animal for her korban, her vow turned out void, and it reverted to him. The card, given only for the son's need, returned to the shared inheritance.
inheritance/gift-given-for-a-specific-ne.description: Does a gift given for a specific need go back once the need is gone? The Rogatchover Gaon rules on an army exemption card, based on Nazir 24a.

inheritance/paying-off-a-parents-debts.intro: A father died owing 100 zuz and left land worth 50 zuz, which beis din gave to the creditor. The orphans quietly paid him 50 zuz to buy the land back, but he kept it, saying he assumed they were paying off the rest of their father's debt. Abaye in Kesubos 91b sided with the creditor, telling the orphans they had merited the mitzvah of settling their father's debt.
inheritance/paying-off-a-parents-debts.description: Heirs gave a creditor 50 zuz without saying why. Did it buy back the land or pay their father's debt? Abaye rules on the orphans' case in Kesubos 91b.

avadim/eved-ivri-gets-the-only-pillow.intro: Kiddushin 20a teaches that buying an eved Ivri is like buying a master for oneself. Tosefos explain that if the master has only one pillow, he must give it to the servant and rest his own head on the ground, yet in Bava Metzia the owner of the water keeps it for himself. The Maharam Schiff resolves this contradiction between the two uses of the word imach.
avadim/eved-ivri-gets-the-only-pillow.description: Why must a master with one pillow give it to his eved Ivri? Tosefos and the Maharam Schiff explain buying a master for oneself in Kiddushin 20a.

avadim/eved-ivri-who-becomes-ill.intro: A master hired an eved Ivri for six years, but the servant spent two of them sick in bed. Kiddushin 17a rules that the master cannot demand a refund, since it is his bad mazal. Tosfos explain that buying an eved Ivri gives the master a lien on the servant himself, like a leased car he cannot drive, while an ordinary worker is paid only for work done.
avadim/eved-ivri-who-becomes-ill.description: Why can't a master demand money back when his eved Ivri falls ill? Tosfos explain how he differs from an ordinary hired worker in Kiddushin 17a.

avadim/eved-kenani-status.intro: An eved Kenani must keep most mitzvos, and once he is freed he becomes a full Jew. The Kli Chemda uses this to suggest a surprise: Haman sold himself as a slave to Mordechai, so his descendants could join the Jewish people. [Haman’s Sons in Bnei Brak](/daf/sanhedrin/96/hamans-sons-in-bnei-brak) brings this idea from Sanhedrin 96b, along with the Chasam Sofer's reading of why Mordechai would not bow.
avadim/eved-kenani-status.description: An eved Kenani keeps most mitzvos and becomes fully Jewish when freed. The Kli Chemda says Haman was Mordechai's slave, tied to Sanhedrin 96b's teaching.

vows-and-oaths/annulling-a-vow-with-a-pe.intro: A sage can release a vow by finding a pesach, an opening, showing that the person did not consider some fact that would have stopped him from vowing. The Mishnah in Nedarim 65b gives examples, such as not realizing the vow violated the prohibition against revenge or bearing a grudge, and [What Makes a Valid Pesach?](/daf/nedarim/65/what-makes-a-valid-pesach) explains why this works for vows but never for a sale or a marriage.
vows-and-oaths/annulling-a-vow-with-a-pe.description: How does a sage annul a vow with a pesach, an opening the vower had not considered? The Mishnah in Nedarim 65b and why it works only for vows.

vows-and-oaths/annulling-future-vows.intro: Part of the erev Rosh Hashanah hataras nedarim declares that vows made in the coming year will be void. The Gemara relates that Rav Huna wanted to teach this publicly, but Rava stopped him, because the Mishnah hid the idea and people might start taking vows lightly. The article on Nedarim 23 adds that, according to the Ran, Kol Nidrei was also worded somewhat confusingly for the same reason.
vows-and-oaths/annulling-future-vows.description: Can you cancel next year's vows in advance? Why Rava stopped Rav Huna from teaching it publicly, and the limits people overlook. Nedarim 23.

vows-and-oaths/annulling-vows-based-on-n.intro: The Mishnah rules that a pesach cannot rest on something that happened after the vow, like the person later becoming the town scribe. Yet the article on Nedarim 65b shows that Moshe's oath was released because Dasan and Aviram lost their wealth after he swore. Most Rishonim answer that a new circumstance works if it was foreseeable, and Tosfos say the same about Kalba Savua's vow against Rebbe Akiva.
vows-and-oaths/annulling-vows-based-on-n.description: Can events after a vow be grounds to annul it? Moshe's oath and Kalba Savua's vow show the Rishonim's rule of foreseeable change. Nedarim 65b.

vows-and-oaths/annulling-vows-on-shabbos.intro: A beis din is not convened on Shabbos to annul vows, unless the vow keeps a person from enjoying Shabbos. The article on Nedarim 77 lists examples from the Mishnah Berurah and other poskim: vows not to eat meat, drink wine, sleep, eat challah or take a stroll, along with vows that stop someone from going to shul or learning Torah. The Biur Halachah still prefers annulling such vows before Shabbos.
vows-and-oaths/annulling-vows-on-shabbos.description: When may a vow be annulled on Shabbos? Vows against meat, wine, sleep, challah or a stroll, and vows that block a mitzvah, discussed on Nedarim 77.

vows-and-oaths/annulling-your-own-vow.intro: Why can't a person simply find his own pesach and release his own vow? The article on Nedarim 65b explains that the Gemara in Chagigah requires going to someone else, even if one knows the sage's reasoning. Yet on Nedarim 64b, the commentator printed as Rashi suggests Moshe released himself from his oath; the Bach calls this a textual error, while the Shaar HaMelech allows it in rare cases.
vows-and-oaths/annulling-your-own-vow.description: Can a scholar release himself from his own vow? The Gemara requires another sage, but the Shaar HaMelech allows rare exceptions. Nedarim 64b and 65b.

vows-and-oaths/default-length-of-nezirus.intro: The man in the Mishnah who said this cow said I am a nazir if I stand never named a time period, so how long is he a nazir? The halacha is that a vow without a stated term lasts thirty days, during which he may not drink wine, cut his hair or touch the dead, as [How Now Brown Cow?](/daf/nazir/10/how-now-brown-cow) explains on Nazir 10a.
vows-and-oaths/default-length-of-nezirus.description: How long does a nazir vow last when no time period is stated? Thirty days, as a playful look at the talking cow case in the Mishnah of Nazir 10a explains.

vows-and-oaths/giving-a-dowry-despite-a-.intro: Reuven forbade his brother Shimon from benefiting from his liquor, then traded the liquor for dried fruit. Years later he offered the fruit as a dowry for Shimon's daughter. Building on Nedarim 57a, the Chasam Sofer ruled that even if the fruit were forbidden to Shimon, a father has no enforceable duty to give a dowry, so only the chassan and kallah benefit, much like feeding a person's young children.
vows-and-oaths/giving-a-dowry-despite-a-.description: May property forbidden to a father by vow be given as his daughter's dowry? The Chasam Sofer says the couple, not the father, benefits. Nedarim 57a.

vows-and-oaths/hataras-nedarim-with-gene.intro: Nedarim 76b tells, without explanation, that Chiya the son of Rav would shoot arrows, and Rabba the son of Rav Huna would sit and stand. Most Rishonim read these as cases of releasing vows through general regret, like saying the vow was made in a bad mood, rather than through a specific pesach. [Of Arrows and Annulments](/daf/nedarim/76/of-arrows-and-annulments) explains why such a release takes no longer than shooting an arrow.
vows-and-oaths/hataras-nedarim-with-gene.description: Can a vow be released just by saying you regret it? Most Rishonim read the arrows of Chiya and Rabba in Nedarim 76b as cases of general regret.

vows-and-oaths/husband-annulling-wifes-v.intro: The Torah lets a husband cancel some of his wife's vows on his own, without going to a sage or beis din. As the article on Nedarim 76b explains, this right covers vows that cause her affliction or that interfere with their relationship, and it lasts only one day. The accepted halacha is that he may annul only on the halachic calendar day he hears the vow.
vows-and-oaths/husband-annulling-wifes-v.description: Which of his wife's vows may a husband cancel on his own, and until when? The Torah's special right and its one-day limit, explained on Nedarim 76b.

vows-and-oaths/intending-to-sin-without-.intro: A woman broke her vow without knowing her husband had already annulled it, and the Torah still says she needs forgiveness. Nazir 23a records that Rebbe Akiva cried at this verse: if one who meant to eat pig meat but ate sheep needs atonement, how much more one who actually ate pig. Intent to sin alone requires atonement.
vows-and-oaths/intending-to-sin-without-.description: Why does someone who thought he broke a vow that was already annulled still need atonement? Rebbe Akiva's tears over intent to sin, in Nazir 23a.

vows-and-oaths/leftover-meat-after-a-vow.intro: The Rosh explains that an unresolved question in Chullin 17a matters today. Meat that was permitted in the desert was later brought into Eretz Yisrael, where shechitah was required. So too, a person who vowed off meat from a certain date may wonder if meat already in his fridge keeps its permitted status, though some Acharonim limit the comparison.
vows-and-oaths/leftover-meat-after-a-vow.description: May meat you already own be eaten after a vow against meat takes effect? The Rosh's comparison to desert meat entering Eretz Yisrael. From Chullin 17a.

vows-and-oaths/nazir-olam.intro: A Nazir Olam takes on lifelong nezirus and may not enter a cemetery, yet he has two big leniencies over a Nazir Shimshon. He may take a haircut now and then, and if his nezirus becomes unbearable he may be released through hataras nedarim. Nazir 14a teaches that a Nazir Shimshon has no such escape route.
vows-and-oaths/nazir-olam.description: How does a Nazir Olam differ from a Nazir Shimshon? He may cut his hair now and then and be released by hataras nedarim, as Nazir 14a teaches.

vows-and-oaths/nazir-shimshon.intro: A Nazir Shimshon avoids grape products and haircuts for life, but not tumah, and Nazir 14a says his vow cannot be undone through hataras nedarim. So why do many hataras nedarim texts on Erev Rosh Hashana ask release from Nezirus Shimshon vows? [Nezirus and Annulling Vows](/daf/nazir/14/nezirus-and-annulling-vows) brings defenses from the Mabit, the Ri Migash and the Nidrei Zrizin.
vows-and-oaths/nazir-shimshon.description: What is a Nazir Shimshon, and why can't his lifelong vow be annulled? Nazir 14a, Dayan Weiss's case and the hataras nedarim text on Erev Rosh Hashana.

vows-and-oaths/neder-versus-shevuah.intro: A neder forbids the use of an object, while a shevuah binds a person to do or not do an action, such as sleeping. So why does the Gemara on Nedarim 8 call a commitment to learn a tractate a neder? [Loath To Make An Oath](/daf/nedarim/8/loath-to-make-an-oath) brings the Ran's answer that the terms are sometimes used interchangeably, even though the two concepts remain different.
vows-and-oaths/neder-versus-shevuah.description: What is the difference between a neder and a shevuah? One forbids an object, the other binds a person to act, and Nedarim 8 shows where they overlap.

vows-and-oaths/nezirus-nowadays.intro: Since the Churban, nezirim have been almost unheard of, apart from rare cases of someone who made a nazir vow without meaning to, and some suggest that is why Nazir has an unusual text and no true Rashi. Even so, a practical lesson remains, and [Where Is Rashi?](/daf/nazir/24/where-is-rashi) finds one in Nazir 24a about an army exemption card.
vows-and-oaths/nezirus-nowadays.description: Why are nazirite vows almost unknown since the Churban, and what lessons remain? The text of Nazir and a ruling on an army card from Nazir 24a.

vows-and-oaths/oath-before-yom-kippur-to.intro: Rav Elyashiv reported that Rav Yisrael Salanter had people swear, before Yom Kippur, not to eat a date's volume of food. Then the Yom Kippur ban could not take hold, and the Chiddushei HaRan says half a shiur under an oath is allowed. In this discussion on Shevuos 28, Rav Elyashiv warns that the Ran later agreed with the Rambam, yet the trick still turns a kareis sin into a lighter one.
vows-and-oaths/oath-before-yom-kippur-to.description: Can an oath before Yom Kippur make eating small amounts a lighter sin? The Chiddushei HaRan, the Rambam and Rav Elyashiv, in an article on Shevuos 28.

vows-and-oaths/oath-not-to-sleep-for-thr.intro: An oath not to sleep for three days is a vain oath, since no one can stay awake that long. So how could Dovid HaMelech vow not to sleep until he found the place of the Beis HaMikdash, as Zevachim 54b describes? The Shita Mekubetzes says he only gave up sleeping in his own bed, and the Har Tzvi notes that his vow could have been fulfilled within three days.
vows-and-oaths/oath-not-to-sleep-for-thr.description: An oath not to sleep for three days is a vain oath. How could Dovid HaMelech vow not to sleep until he found the Beis HaMikdash site, in Zevachim 54b?

vows-and-oaths/oaths-over-land-and-attac.intro: An owner says he gave a watchman ten vines full of grapes, and the watchman says it was only five. Beis din does not make anyone swear over real estate, and vines count as land. In Shevuos 42b, the chachamim say grapes on the vine are like land, while Rebbe Meir says ripe grapes are like picked fruit, so the watchman can be made to swear.
vows-and-oaths/oaths-over-land-and-attac.description: Why does beis din not impose oaths over land, and are ripe grapes on the vine land or goods? Rebbe Meir and the chachamim debate in Shevuos 42b.

vows-and-oaths/promises-made-to-a-dying-.intro: Is a promise made just to calm a dying person binding? The Rema rules that a wife who swore to her dying husband never to remarry need not keep it, much like an oath made under duress. On Bava Basra 147b, the Shvus Yaakov says children may be different, while the Mahari Asad, relying on the Ramban, disagrees, so the question remains in dispute.
vows-and-oaths/promises-made-to-a-dying-.description: Is an oath made only to calm a dying person binding? The Rema says no, but the Shvus Yaakov holds children to more. A dispute discussed on Bava Basra 147b.

vows-and-oaths/repeating-a-statement-twi.intro: The Gemara on Shevuos 36 learns from Hashem's promise never to flood the world again that saying I will or I will not can be an oath. Rava says it must be said twice. The Rashba requires intent, Tosfos sees only a moral warning, and the Shulchan Aruch follows the Rashba and the Rosh: intent is needed and the two must be said one after the other.
vows-and-oaths/repeating-a-statement-twi.description: Does saying I will or I will not twice make a binding oath? Rava, the Rashba, Tosfos and the Shulchan Aruch on intent and wording, in Shevuos 36.

vows-and-oaths/saying-bli-neder.intro: People say bli neder all the time, even when ordering chicken at a restaurant, but the phrase has real meaning. A commitment to a mitzvah may count as a vow, and Tosfos holds that saying something twice carries extra weight even without intent. The article on Shevuos 36 shows why adding bli neder makes clear that a promise is only one's word.
vows-and-oaths/saying-bli-neder.description: Why do people add bli neder when promising a good deed? A plain promise to do a mitzvah may count as a vow, as the article on Shevuos 36 explains.

vows-and-oaths/time-limit-for-annulling-.intro: The Mishnah says a husband may annul his wife's vow only until sunset of the day he hears it, while Rebbe Yose the son of Rebbe Yehuda and Rebbe Elazar the son of Rebbe Shimon give him a full 24 hours. The Rosh reads Nedarim 76b as following the second view: Chiya shot an arrow into the wall as a sundial to know when 24 hours had passed. Most Rishonim, and the halacha, disagree.
vows-and-oaths/time-limit-for-annulling-.description: Does a husband have until nightfall or a full 24 hours to cancel a vow? The Rosh explains why Chiya shot an arrow into the wall in Nedarim 76b.

vows-and-oaths/unusual-wording-of-a-nazi.intro: A man says, this cow said I am a nazir if I stand, and Beis Shammai says he becomes a nazir, even though cows don't talk. Nazir 10a explains that he was imagining what the cow would say, and Tosfos compares it to the boat in Yonah that thought it would break. [Holy Cow](/daf/nazir/10/holy-cow) shows that his words were awkward but his intent was clear.
vows-and-oaths/unusual-wording-of-a-nazi.description: How can saying that a cow said I am a nazir count as a real vow? Beis Shammai, the Gemara and Tosfos explain oddly worded nezirus in Nazir 10a.

vows-and-oaths/vague-vows-to-donate-to-h.intro: What must a person give if he vows gold or iron to the Beis Hamikdash without naming an amount? The Mishna sets gold at a Golden Dinar, and a beraisa in Menachos 107a sets iron at enough for a kalya orev, one amah by one amah. Rabbi Akiva Eiger explains that since there is no maximum, the donor must have meant the minimum usable amount.
vows-and-oaths/vague-vows-to-donate-to-h.description: How much must one give after vowing gold or iron to the Beis Hamikdash with no amount named? The Mishna and a beraisa set the minimum in Menachos 107a.

vows-and-oaths/vow-against-eating-meat.intro: Someone vowed to stop eating meat from a set date, and when the day came, his fridge was full. May he finish it off, or must he stop at once? In [Gefilte Fish, Cottage Cheese, And Scotch](/daf/chullin/17/gefilte-fish-cottage-cheese-and-scotch), the Rosh says this is the real case behind the unresolved question in Chullin 17a about desert meat brought into Eretz Yisrael.
vows-and-oaths/vow-against-eating-meat.description: If you vowed to stop eating meat from a set date, may you finish what is in your fridge? The Rosh ties this vow to the unresolved question in Chullin 17a.

vows-and-oaths/vow-conditional-on-a-gift.intro: Reuven vows that Shimon may not benefit from him unless Shimon gives him a sizeable present. Nedarim 24a rules that Reuven can release the vow on his own by declaring, "It is as if I received the present." The Ran says the vow's goal of improving his finances is considered met, while the Rashba reasons that handing over a gift only to return it would be an exercise in futility.
vows-and-oaths/vow-conditional-on-a-gift.description: A vow forbids benefit unless a gift is given. Nedarim 24a lets the vower say it is as if he received it, and the Ran and Rashba explain why.

vows-and-oaths/vow-on-exchanged-items.intro: The Mishnah in Nedarim 57a teaches that when fruits forbidden by a vow are exchanged, the new item can be forbidden as well. [Is Dried Fruit the Top Banana?](/daf/nedarim/57/is-dried-fruit-the-top-banana) brings the Chasam Sofer's case of schnapps traded for dried fruit, where he ruled that it depends on the vower's intent: Reuven only meant to stop his brother's drinking, so the prohibition does not pass to the fruit.
vows-and-oaths/vow-on-exchanged-items.description: Does a vow on one item carry over to what it is traded for? The Mishnah in Nedarim 57a and the Chasam Sofer's ruling on schnapps and dried fruit.

vows-and-oaths/vow-to-move-to-eretz-yisr.intro: A man in trouble vowed, using the word neder, to move to Eretz Yisrael, but by the time he had to go, war made the sea voyage dangerous. The Maharam Padua, building on the Ran and Tosfos on Nedarim 8, reasoned that a neder cannot take hold on an action, even a mitzvah. Yet he hesitated to rule against the Rosh, who holds such a vow binding, writing that the Rosh would crush his skull.
vows-and-oaths/vow-to-move-to-eretz-yisr.description: Is a neder to move to Eretz Yisrael binding when the trip becomes dangerous? The Maharam Padua weighs the Ran against the Rosh, on Nedarim 8.

parnassah/following-your-fathers-trade.intro: Rebbe Yochanan teaches on Arachin 16b that a person should not leave his own trade or his father's, but he gives no reason. The Ben Yehoyada offers three: loyal customers, a heart that is at home in a familiar trade, and the many specific prayers a father said for his son's success. A local shoe repairman who followed his father and grandfather from Samarkand shows the idea in practice.
parnassah/following-your-fathers-trade.description: Why not leave your father's trade? Rebbe Yochanan's advice on Arachin 16b and the Ben Yehoyada's three reasons, including a father's specific prayers.

parnassah/trusting-hashem-for-parnassah.intro: When Elisha made the water of Yericho sweet, the young men who sold drinking water lost their business, and they mocked him. Sotah 46b calls them katanim, meaning people of little faith who did not trust Hashem to give them another living. In [A Miracle Within a Miracle](/daf/sotah/46/a-miracle-within-a-miracle), the Steipler teaches that Hashem is not limited by market forces.
parnassah/trusting-hashem-for-parnassah.description: Does our livelihood come from Hashem or from the market? Sotah 46b on the water sellers who mocked Elisha, and the Steipler's lesson on parnassah.

beis-din/compromise-in-beis-din.intro: Should judges push litigants toward a compromise? Sanhedrin 6a records Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Yose HaGlili, who says compromising is forbidden and the judgment must pierce the mountain. Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai reads the verse as referring to the Golden Calf instead, and practical halacha does encourage compromise.
beis-din/compromise-in-beis-din.description: Should beis din encourage compromise or rule strictly by law? Rabbi Elazar's objection and Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai's reply in Sanhedrin 6a.

beis-din/death-penalty-in-beis-din.intro: A capital case before the Sanhedrin was so demanding that executions were rare. Following the Rambam, [Hitting Rock Bottom](/daf/sanhedrin/44/hitting-rock-bottom) walks through the steps around Sanhedrin 44: questioning the witnesses, sleeping on the verdict, needing a majority of two, and leading the condemned man far from beis din so he could still plead. Stoning itself began with a fall from a platform, then a large stone.
beis-din/death-penalty-in-beis-din.description: How did a Sanhedrin try a capital case? The Rambam's steps from witnesses to deliberation, voting and stoning, and why executions were rare. Sanhedrin 44.

beis-din/disagreeing-with-a-mistaken-psa.intro: The first Mishnah in Horayos 2 teaches that someone who knows the Sanhedrin ruled wrongly may not rely on its psak. The Rashash asks how this fits with the command to obey the court even if it says right is left. He answers that such a person must go to the Sanhedrin and explain his view, and only if they still disagree must he accept their ruling.
beis-din/disagreeing-with-a-mistaken-psa.description: May someone who knows the Sanhedrin ruled wrongly follow its psak? The Mishnah in Horayos 2 and the Rashash on his duty to present his view to the court.

beis-din/humane-execution-by-beis-din.intro: The Gemara in Kesubos 37b uses the verse to love your neighbor as yourself in a surprising place: beis din must choose the least painful and least disfiguring way to carry out an execution. The Ramah in Sanhedrin 52b sees this as proof that the mitzvah covers even a wicked man. The Beis Shearim suggests the condemned man has likely repented.
beis-din/humane-execution-by-beis-din.description: Why must beis din choose the least painful method of execution? Kesubos 37b applies love your neighbor as yourself, and the Ramah in Sanhedrin 52b agrees.

beis-din/litigants-dressed-unequally-in-.intro: Two people come to beis din, one dressed in clothing worth 100 maneh and the other in rags. Shevuos 31a tells the judge to say to the rich one: change into plain clothes or dress your opponent as well as you are. The Ben Yehoyada says this holds even if the poor man brought the case, though it is better for the rich one to dress down.
beis-din/litigants-dressed-unequally-in-.description: Why must a rich litigant dress down or clothe his poor opponent in beis din? Shevuos 31a and the Ben Yehoyada on keeping judges from being swayed.

beis-din/pierson-v-post-in-halacha.intro: In 1802, Lodowick Post's dogs were chasing a fox when Jesse Pierson killed it and carried it off, and the New York court ruled for Pierson. How would a beis din decide? [Catch 22](/daf/gittin/59/catch-22) applies the Mishnah in Gittin 59b and finds that even wounding or snaring an animal is not always enough to acquire it, unless one follows the Ketzos HaChoshen.
beis-din/pierson-v-post-in-halacha.description: How would a beis din rule in Pierson v. Post, the famous hunted fox case? The Mishnah in Gittin 59b and the Ketzos HaChoshen compared with the court.

beis-din/shtar-modaa-protest-document.intro: A shtar modaa is a protest signed before witnesses, saying that an agreement about to be made is under duress. A family pressured into an unfair deal used one, though the witnesses had no firsthand knowledge of the pressure. Building on Bava Basra 48, the article weighs the Rashba, Rabbeinu Yona, and the Rema, who rules that once written, such a modaa is valid after the fact.
beis-din/shtar-modaa-protest-document.description: A shtar modaa protests a forced deal in advance. Must the witnesses know the duress firsthand? The Rashba and Rema, in a case built on Bava Basra 48.

beis-din/unanimous-guilty-verdict-acquit.intro: One of the most striking rules of a capital case is that if every judge votes guilty, the accused goes free. The article on Sanhedrin 44 explains that a guilty verdict must come after real due process. If no judge saw any reason to acquit, the deliberations may have been perfunctory, so he cannot be convicted.
beis-din/unanimous-guilty-verdict-acquit.description: Why is a defendant freed if every judge votes guilty? The rule that a capital verdict needs real debate, explained in a recap of the laws, Sanhedrin 44.

testimony/converted-brothers-as-witnesse.intro: Relatives may not testify together, so two brothers can never serve as a pair of witnesses, no matter how honest they are. But Yevamos 22a teaches that a convert is like a newborn child. So two gentile twin brothers who convert are considered unrelated, and they may testify jointly.
testimony/converted-brothers-as-witnesse.description: Can two brothers who converted together testify as a pair? Since a convert is like a newborn, Yevamos 22a treats them as unrelated witnesses.

testimony/proving-a-boy-reached-bar-mitz.intro: Kiddushin 63b says a father is believed that his son has turned thirteen. A dialogue in [Bar Mitzvah Bewilderment](/daf/kiddushin/63/bar-mitzvah-bewilderment) asks who else is believed: the Siddur Bais Oved doubts the boy himself, while the Kaf HaChaim believes him. Tosfos and the Mishnah Berurah trust only the father, even over the Gadol HaDor, and the Rogochover adds the mother.
testimony/proving-a-boy-reached-bar-mitz.description: Who is believed that a boy has turned thirteen: the boy, his father, his mother or a great sage? Tosfos and the Mishnah Berurah, from Kiddushin 63b.

testimony/signing-a-document-with-a-symb.intro: The Gemara in Gittin 36a says Rav signed legal documents by drawing a fish, and everyone knew a fish in place of a signature meant Rav was the witness. Since drawing zodiac signs is forbidden, the Taz and the Shach ask how this was allowed. In [Sounds Fishy](/daf/gittin/36/sounds-fishy), the Taz points to a two-dimensional drawing, while the Shach says one sign alone is fine.
testimony/signing-a-document-with-a-symb.description: May a witness sign a document with a drawing instead of his name? Rav signed with a fish in Gittin 36a, and the Taz and the Shach explain why it was fine.

testimony/single-witness-in-monetary-cas.intro: In Kesubos 85a, Rava accepted his wife's word about a defendant but refused the word of the saintly Rav Papa about a repaid loan. The simple reading is that Rava was unsure of Rav Papa's righteousness. Rav Moshe Feinstein rejects that: even Moshe Rabbeinu as a lone witness is not believed in money matters, but Rava knew firsthand, through years of marriage, that his wife never lied.
testimony/single-witness-in-monetary-cas.description: Why did Rava trust his wife but not Rav Papa as a lone witness? Rav Moshe Feinstein on firsthand knowledge versus general trust, in Kesubos 85a.

testimony/single-witness-in-ritual-matte.intro: Tosfos on Kiddushin 64a say a father is believed about his son's age because one witness is believed in matters other than money and marriage. The Tosfos Rid disagrees, comparing it to the Torah's special trust in a father about his firstborn. Tosfos add that one witness is believed only about things under his control, yet the father is trusted because he knows his son's birthday best.
testimony/single-witness-in-ritual-matte.description: When is one witness believed in non-monetary matters, and why does a father have special credibility? Tosfos and the Tosfos Rid on Kiddushin 64a.

testimony/third-witness-in-eidim-zomemim.intro: Zomemim witnesses receive the very punishment they tried to bring on an innocent person. Two witnesses are already full proof, so a third adds nothing. Yet Rebbe Akiva in Makkos 5b says that if a third witness gives the same false testimony and all are proven liars, he is punished just like the first two, and the article draws a lesson about joining others.
testimony/third-witness-in-eidim-zomemim.description: Why is a third false witness, whose testimony added nothing, punished like the first two? Rebbe Akiva on eidim zomemim in the Mishnah in Makkos 5b.

testimony/warning-before-a-capital-sin.intro: Circumstantial evidence is not valid in Sanhedrin. Witnesses must see the act themselves, and they must first warn the person that it carries the death penalty. In its recap of Sanhedrin 44, the article notes that he has to accept the warning and sin anyway within about four seconds, which is why executions were so rare.
testimony/warning-before-a-capital-sin.description: Before a capital sin, witnesses must see the act and warn the sinner of the penalty, who must sin within seconds. Why executions were rare, Sanhedrin 44.

testimony/witness-who-raised-his-hand-to.intro: Does lifting a hand to hit another Jew disqualify a person as a witness? Based on Sanhedrin 58b, the Beis Yosef says he is rabbinically invalid, and the Chut Hasheni says even biblically. Rav Zilberstein, citing the Pischei Teshuvah and the Maharshal, rules that one provoked by public verbal abuse is not called a rasha and stays a valid witness.
testimony/witness-who-raised-his-hand-to.description: Is a man who raises his hand to strike disqualified as a witness? Sanhedrin 58b, the Beis Yosef, and Rav Zilberstein on how provocation changes the ruling.

shlichus/doing-a-mitzvah-yourself-versus.intro: It is a greater mitzvah to do a commandment yourself than through a messenger. The Chida says that is why Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi, personally bought the cow for his son's wedding, a story in Makkos 14a. The Magen Avraham applies the rule to all mitzvos, while the Machzik Berachah says it does not cover preparing meals like a wedding feast, which are not the mitzvah itself.
shlichus/doing-a-mitzvah-yourself-versus.description: Is a mitzvah done yourself greater than one done by an agent? The Chida, Magen Avraham and Machzik Berachah on Rabban Gamliel's cow, from Makkos 14a.

psak-halacha/ad-velo-ad-bichlal.intro: In 2005, a Boro Park homeowner got a sidewalk ticket at exactly 9:00 a.m., when the law allowed tickets from 8 to 9, and on appeal he won. The Gemara calls this logic ad v'lo ad bichlal, until but not including. As the article on Menachos 68 shows, Rav and Shmuel read the pasuk about new grain this way, while Rebbe Yehudah holds until and including.
psak-halacha/ad-velo-ad-bichlal.description: Does until include the last moment? A Boro Park sidewalk ticket shows ad v'lo ad bichlal, the root of a dispute over new grain in Menachos 68.

psak-halacha/applying-talmudic-principle.intro: How could Rav Moshe Feinstein rule on toiveling a toaster or using a hearing aid on Shabbos, when the Gemara never mentions them? As his teshuvos show, he drew principles from earlier sources and applied them to the new question. [Da’as Torah](/daf/bava-metzia/33/daas-torah), filed on Bava Metzia 33, brings Rav Henoch Leibowitz's point that daas Torah works the same way.
psak-halacha/applying-talmudic-principle.description: How do poskim rule on toasters, hearing aids and IVF, which the Gemara never discusses? Rav Moshe applied principles from older sources, Bava Metzia 33.

psak-halacha/authorship-of-the-mishnah-b.intro: The Mishnah Berurah seems to contradict itself about davening on leaves on Yom Kippur. The Chofetz Chaim's son revealed that he wrote parts of the work himself and sent them to his father and Rabbi Tzvi for review, and warned that certain contradictions may result. There is also a tradition that Rav Dovid Leibowitz wrote Hilchos Sukkah, notes a discussion of Zevachim 46.
psak-halacha/authorship-of-the-mishnah-b.description: Did the Chofetz Chaim write every part of the Mishnah Berurah? His son's testimony may explain some contradictions, in a discussion tied to Zevachim 46.

psak-halacha/choosing-the-lesser-of-two-.intro: May someone facing two forbidden paths choose the lighter one? The Meiri says one may never tell others a sin is permitted to save them from a worse one, yet the Beis Shmuel and Chelkas Mechokek allow a person to make that calculation for himself. [Choosing The Lesser Evil](/daf/sanhedrin/6/choosing-the-lesser-evil) applies this, from Sanhedrin 6a, to a bachur who would rather stay in bed than smoke on Shabbos.
psak-halacha/choosing-the-lesser-of-two-.description: May you choose the lesser of two sins, or tell others to? The Meiri, the Beis Shmuel and a bachur tempted to smoke on Shabbos, from Sanhedrin 6a.

psak-halacha/divine-help-in-reaching-the.intro: The last Mishnah in Bava Basra praises Shimon ben Nanas as the master of monetary law, in the very place the halacha does not follow him. The Satmar Rebbe, as Sanhedrin 2 begins, explains that even after all one's effort, reaching the true halacha takes Divine help and prayer. The Vilna Gaon told the Teshuvos Shmuel much the same: brilliance alone does not guarantee the right psak.
psak-halacha/divine-help-in-reaching-the.description: Why praise Shimon ben Nanas where the halacha rejects him? The Satmar Rebbe says great scholars need Divine help for the right psak. Read with Sanhedrin 2.

psak-halacha/following-the-later-talmudi.intro: When two Amoraim disagree, halacha usually follows the later one, who heard all the debate in the beis midrash. The Birkei Yosef applies this to Rava and Rav Nachman on Hallel in Megillah 14a. But the Shivas Tzion points to the Rif, who rules like Rav Nachman when his own student Rava argued with him directly, and the Nemukei Yosef says it depends on the exact text.
psak-halacha/following-the-later-talmudi.description: Does halacha follow the later Amora, even when a student argues with his rebbe? The Birkei Yosef, the Rif and Rava versus Rav Nachman in Megillah 14a.

psak-halacha/halacha-follows-an-anonymou.intro: The Gemara on Eruvin 13 says no one in Rebbe Meir's generation equaled him, yet the halacha does not follow him. But Rebbe Yochanan ruled that the halacha follows an anonymous Mishnah, and Rav Sherira Gaon says Rebbe built the mishnayos on Rebbe Meir's teachings. So the halacha often does follow him, and the Ben Yehoyada explains why it could not always.
psak-halacha/halacha-follows-an-anonymou.description: Why does the halacha follow an anonymous Mishnah, and how does that fit Rebbe Meir? Rebbe Yochanan's rule and Rav Sherira Gaon's view, from Eruvin 13.

psak-halacha/halacha-veein-morin-kein.intro: Some laws are permitted but may not be taught publicly, known as halacha v'ein morin kein. On Beitzah 28a, Rabbah would not reveal his ruling even to Abaye, his own student. Rabbi Yehonason Eibshitz says it may be told to individuals, but the Mishna Berura forbids teaching it even to a student, and the Shulchan Aruch HaRav allows it within the study of a topic.
psak-halacha/halacha-veein-morin-kein.description: What are laws that are permitted but may not be taught, and how do we know them? Rabbah, the Mishna Berura and others explain, from Beitzah 28a.

psak-halacha/kavod-habriyos-and-halacha.intro: Why may a clogged toilet be cleared on Shabbos without great loss, when the gutter in Kesubos 60a needed both a shinui and the threat of a flood? Some suggest kavod habriyos, human dignity, which in limited cases even overrides a Torah precept. Not being able to use a toilet is like a great loss, though this reason would not cover a sink.
psak-halacha/kavod-habriyos-and-halacha.description: How can human dignity set aside a rabbinic prohibition? Kavod habriyos may explain clearing a blocked toilet on Shabbos, in contrast to Kesubos 60a.

psak-halacha/meaning-of-teiku.intro: When the Gemara cannot settle a question, it says Teiku, simply meaning the question stands. The Tosfos Yom Tov reads it as an acronym: Eliyahu will answer the open questions when Moshiach comes. In [Eliyahu HaNavi Zachur La’Tov](/daf/bava-metzia/114/eliyahu-hanavi-zachur-latov), Bava Metzia 114b shows that Tosfos does not always follow Eliyahu's answers.
psak-halacha/meaning-of-teiku.description: What does Teiku mean? The Tosfos Yom Tov reads it as Eliyahu answering all open questions, yet Tosfos does not always follow him, in Bava Metzia 114b.

psak-halacha/one-rabbi-overturning-anoth.intro: In Chullin 44b, Rav examined an animal with a cut windpipe and seemed to rule it treif, yet Rabba bar bar Chana later permitted it and bought its meat. Once a scholar forbids something, another may not permit it. Rashi in Niddah 20b says this is about respect, while the Raavad and Ritva say the ruling changes the object itself.
psak-halacha/one-rabbi-overturning-anoth.description: Why can't a rabbi permit what a colleague forbade, and may he reverse his own ruling? Rashi, the Raavad and the Ritva differ. Chullin 44b and Niddah 20b.

psak-halacha/order-of-items-in-a-mishnah.intro: Can halacha be learned from the order in which a Mishnah lists things? Rav Huna says generally not, though the Mishnah on Sanhedrin 49b, listing punishments from stoning down, is precise, while the kohen's garments are not listed in dressing order. The Tevuos Shor suggests the marror list in Pesachim 39a is also precise, which is why the Shulchan Aruch prefers chazeres.
psak-halacha/order-of-items-in-a-mishnah.description: Does the order of a Mishnah's list matter in halacha? Rav Huna, the punishments of Sanhedrin 49b, the kohen's garments and marror in Pesachim 39a.

psak-halacha/paskening-after-drinking-wi.intro: Shmuel taught that someone who drinks a revi'is of wine may not give halachic rulings. Rav Nachman objected that his mind is not clear until he drinks a revi'is, and Rava rebuked him for calling any teaching not good. In [It’s All Good](/daf/eruvin/64/its-all-good), on Eruvin 64, this exchange opens a debate about how one may speak of words of Torah.
psak-halacha/paskening-after-drinking-wi.description: May someone who has drunk a revi'is of wine give halachic rulings? Shmuel's rule, Rav Nachman's objection and Rava's rebuke, in the Gemara on Eruvin 64.

psak-halacha/what-counts-as-a-language-i.intro: Could someone daven in Klingon, the made-up language of Star Trek? The Ran in Nedarim 2a defines a language as a way of speaking used by a group of people by convention. In [Can One Daven in Klingon?](/daf/sotah/33/can-one-daven-in-klingon), the Chofetz Chaim's rule that people nearby must speak it, and the seventy languages of the Sanhedrin, suggest the answer is no.
psak-halacha/what-counts-as-a-language-i.description: What counts as a real language in halacha? The Ran in Nedarim 2a defines one, and the Chofetz Chaim's rule shows why Klingon prayers would not pass.

safek/checking-every-chicken-for-treifos.intro: Halacha normally relies on rov, assuming most birds are healthy, but once a defect passes about ten percent, that reliance is suspended. With torn tendons now common, some hashgachos check a few hundred birds each morning and rely on the result. [The Tendon Tempest](/daf/chullin/57/the-tendon-tempest) reports that stricter processors check every bird, building on Chullin 57a.
safek/checking-every-chicken-for-treifos.description: Can a kosher plant rely on a morning sample, or must every chicken be checked for torn tendons? Rov, the ten percent threshold and Chullin 57a.

safek/doubts-eliyahu-will-resolve.intro: On Bechoros 27, a creature that looks like a piglet is seen nursing from a sheep, and no one knows if it is the sheep's offspring or a real pig. The Gemara leaves it forbidden until Eliyahu HaNavi comes to decide. The Yad Eliyahu uses this against the idea that pork will be allowed in the future, but Eruvin 43a shows Eliyahu comes before Moshiach.
safek/doubts-eliyahu-will-resolve.description: A pig-like animal nursing from a sheep stays forbidden until Eliyahu comes. Bechoros 27 and Eruvin 43a shape the debate over pork in the future.

safek/majority-and-fixed-location-in-dou.intro: Most of the land below a plane is not a Jewish cemetery, so may a kohen rely on the majority? In [Grave Concerns](/daf/nazir/59/grave-concerns), on Nazir 59, Shimon explains that we follow the majority for meat found outside many butcher shops, which is not in its place. A grave is kavua, fixed in its place, so the doubt may be treated as an even 50-50 safek.
safek/majority-and-fixed-location-in-dou.description: When do we follow the majority in a doubt, and why is a fixed grave different? Rov and kavua, in a story of a kohen on a plane, in an article on Nazir 59.

safek/safek-derabbanan-lekula.intro: Doubts in Torah law are treated strictly, while doubts in rabbinic law are often treated leniently. On Nedarim 80b, the article applies this to shoes on Yom Kippur that might be leather, which Tosfos would permit and the Rambam would forbid. Rebbe Akiva Eiger builds a double doubt, a sfeik sfaika, working through the possibilities like a math problem with an order of operations.
safek/safek-derabbanan-lekula.description: Why are doubts in rabbinic law treated leniently and Torah doubts strictly? Leather shoes on Yom Kippur and Rebbe Akiva Eiger's double doubt. Nedarim 80b.

rabbinic-decrees/food-owned-before-a-ban.intro: In Europe, rabbanim sometimes banned fish on Shabbos when fishmongers raised prices. The Mishnah Berurah rules that gefilte fish already in the freezer may still be served. [Kosher Questions](/daf/chullin/17/kosher-questions) suggests a source in Chullin 17a: the unresolved question of permitted desert meat brought into Eretz Yisrael, since in a rabbinic doubt we may be lenient.
rabbinic-decrees/food-owned-before-a-ban.description: May food bought before a rabbinic ban still be eaten? The Mishnah Berurah on fish already in the freezer and a source in Chullin 17a. A kashrus question.

rabbinic-decrees/maaris-ayin.intro: Some acts are permitted, yet the Sages worried about how they look to others. Tosfos on Yevamos 21a apply this concern, called maaris ayin, to marrying a father-in-law's former wife, which might look like marrying a mother-in-law. They also apply it to step-siblings who might look like brother and sister, though there the Bavli assumes everyone knows the truth.
rabbinic-decrees/maaris-ayin.description: What is maaris ayin? The concern for acts that look forbidden, applied to marrying a father-in-law's widow or a step-sister, in Yevamos 21a.

rabbinic-decrees/rabbinic-control-of-foo.intro: The Sages watched food prices closely. Taanis 15 rules that a series of fasts for rain does not begin on a Thursday, since the extra shopping could push merchants to raise prices. In Bava Basra 96a, when a pair of birds for korbanos cost a gold dinar, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel vowed not to sleep until the price fell, and his ruling dropped it to a hundredth.
rabbinic-decrees/rabbinic-control-of-foo.description: Did the Sages step in on food prices? Why fasts for rain avoid Thursdays in Taanis 15, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's bird ruling in Bava Basra 96a.

rabbinic-decrees/raising-a-ben-pekua-her.intro: If two ben pekua animals are bred together, their offspring is also a ben pekua. So why not raise a whole herd and skip shechitah altogether? As the story built on Chullin 75b explains, rabbinic law would still require shechitah and keep the gid hanasheh restrictions, but one real advantage remains: a ben pekua with a fatal defect would not become a treifah.
rabbinic-decrees/raising-a-ben-pekua-her.description: Could a herd of ben pekua animals save on shechitah and the hindquarters? Why rabbinic decrees limit the gain, and the treifah advantage, in Chullin 75b.

rabbinic-decrees/raising-chickens-in-yer.intro: The Piskei Tosfos explains why an egg was once worth a perutah: the sages banned raising chickens in Yerushalayim, fearing they would carry tumah onto the paths, so eggs had to be brought in. But Rebbe Shelah in Yoma 20b speaks of a rooster's call there. The Dovev Meisharim answers that chickens in coops were allowed, and only free-range ones were forbidden.
rabbinic-decrees/raising-chickens-in-yer.description: Why was raising chickens banned in Yerushalayim, and how did it raise egg prices? The Piskei Tosfos and Dovev Meisharim, with a rooster in Yoma 20b.

rabbinic-decrees/using-a-dead-tree-on-sh.intro: Does the ban on using trees on Shabbos include dead trees? The Gemara in Eruvin 100a concludes that dead trees are technically allowed, but not in winter, when nobody can tell which trees are alive. Rav forbade all trees in one place lacking Torah knowledge, and while the Shulchan Aruch follows his stringency, the Rosh allows leaning on a dead tree in summer.
rabbinic-decrees/using-a-dead-tree-on-sh.description: Does the Shabbos ban on using trees apply to dead trees? Eruvin 100a on winter, summer and Rav's local rule, as the Shulchan Aruch and the Rosh differ.

rabbinic-decrees/yehoshuas-water-rights-.intro: When Yehoshua divided Eretz Yisrael, he made each inheritance conditional on certain rules, one being that a water source on private land is open to all. Tosfos on Avodah Zarah 59a uses this to ask how any water could be private, and suggests the rule covers only springs and not man-made wells. Tosfos Ri M'Birnaya rules that the enactments bind Jews everywhere, even in Chutz La'aretz.
rabbinic-decrees/yehoshuas-water-rights-.description: Yehoshua's conditions on water sources when Eretz Yisrael was divided: do they apply outside Israel and to dug wells? Tosfos weighs in on Avodah Zarah 59a.

minhagim/avoiding-sour-foods-on-rosh-has.intro: The Mishnah Berurah records customs not to eat sour foods like borscht on Rosh Hashanah, or fish cooked in vinegar, and the Dirshu edition adds bitter or hot foods. [Vital Signs](/daf/sanhedrin/65/vital-signs) asks how this fits with Sanhedrin 65b, which forbids relying on omens. By the Maharsha, avoiding bad omens should be wrong, and with no Yehi Ratzon the Meiri's answer does not fit either.
minhagim/avoiding-sour-foods-on-rosh-has.description: Why do some avoid sour or vinegary foods on Rosh Hashanah? The Mishnah Berurah's customs and how they square with the ban on omens in Sanhedrin 65b.

minhagim/celebrating-birthdays-in-halach.intro: Should Jews celebrate birthdays at all? The Minchas Elazar noted that gedolim did not, citing Eruvin 13b that it would have been better never to be born, though Tosafos on Avodah Zarah 5a say this does not apply to tzaddikim. Others saw it differently: the Chasam Sofer is reported to have made a siyum on his birthday, and the Ben Ish Chai writes that his household made it a joyous day.
minhagim/celebrating-birthdays-in-halach.description: Should Jews celebrate birthdays? The Minchas Elazar, the Chasam Sofer and the Ben Ish Chai differ, with Eruvin 13b and Tosafos on Avodah Zarah 5a.

minhagim/chickpeas-at-a-shalom-zachar.intro: Why are chickpeas or lentils served at a shalom zachar, when they are foods for mourners? The Maharshal and the Derisha explain that the newborn has just lost the Torah he learned in the womb, as taught in Niddah 30b. Guests come to comfort him, and the bris waits until after seven days of mourning for that loss.
minhagim/chickpeas-at-a-shalom-zachar.description: Chickpeas and lentils are mourners' foods. Why serve them at a shalom zachar? The Maharshal and Derisha link it to the Torah a baby forgets, Niddah 30b.

minhagim/following-the-customs-of-a-new-.intro: Rebbe Zaira fasted one hundred fasts to master the Eretz Yisrael way of learning, then moved there. When he ate meat that Bavel considered forbidden, scholars asked why he did not keep his hometown custom. In [A Tale of Two Riddles: The Vacuuming Wife and the Havdala Surprise](/daf/chullin/18/a-tale-of-two-riddles-the-vacuuming-wife-and-the-havdala-surprise), Rav Ashi explains in Chullin 18b that a permanent resident follows his new home, strict or lenient.
minhagim/following-the-customs-of-a-new-.description: Does someone who moves for good follow the customs of his new home? Rav Ashi's answer about Rebbe Zaira, strict or lenient, from Chullin 18b.

minhagim/following-the-customs-of-our-fa.intro: When Yitzchak redug the wells his father Avraham had dug, he gave them the same names his father had used. Rabbeinu Bachye writes that the Torah tells us this as a merit for Yitzchak, and as a lesson not to stray from the paths, customs and mussar of our fathers. [A Matter Of Mesorah](/daf/nedarim/12/a-matter-of-mesorah), filed on Nedarim 12, joins this to Rav Henoch Leibowitz's teaching.
