hakaras-hatov/gratitude-to-those-who-pro.intro: The Torah expects gratitude even to someone who opens a door for us. Rav Chaim Shmuelevitz reasoned that we certainly owe thanks to those who put their lives on the line to protect us, and Rav Asher Weiss notes that these words were truly written by Rav Chaim himself. [A Holy Place in the World to Come](/daf/bava-basra/10/a-holy-place-in-the-world-to-come) links this to Bava Basra 10b and the exalted place of those who die protecting other Jews.
hakaras-hatov/gratitude-to-those-who-pro.description: If we must thank someone who opens a door, how much more those who risk their lives for us? Rav Chaim Shmuelevitz's lesson, linked to Bava Basra 10b.

honesty/admitting-a-mistake.intro: A president once said he might be wrong but would never admit it, and would find some excuse instead. [The Truth of the Matter](/daf/zevachim/101/the-truth-of-the-matter) sets this beside Moshe Rabbeinu, who openly told Aharon he had heard a halacha and forgotten it. Zevachim 101a praises that honesty, and the article adds that the higher a person climbs, the subtler the test of truth becomes.
honesty/admitting-a-mistake.description: Saying "I was wrong" is hard for leaders. Moshe openly admitted he forgot a halacha, and Zevachim 101a praises him for not hiding behind an excuse.

honesty/donating-ill-gotten-money.intro: The Maharsha draws a sharp lesson from Kesubos 66b: people who grow rich dishonestly and pledge large sums for their own glory will not be saved from the punishment of theft. The Chasam Sofer asks where the Gemara even mentions how money was earned. He points to the rain miracle, suggesting Nakdimon should have paid the twelve talents of silver and then gave that very money away for honor.
honesty/donating-ill-gotten-money.description: Can big pledges from dishonest money bring merit? The Maharsha and Chasam Sofer find a warning in the fall of Nakdimon ben Gurion in Kesubos 66b.

honesty/falsifying-torah-to-avoid-danger.intro: Two Roman officers studied the Torah and found one law they objected to, yet the rabbis did not claim the law was different. The Yam Shel Shlomo learns that falsifying the Torah is forbidden even to prevent dangerous decrees. [A Case of Pikuach Nefesh](/daf/bava-kamma/60/a-case-of-pikuach-nefesh), filed on Bava Kamma 60b, applies this to a religious exemption letter full of made-up reasons.
honesty/falsifying-torah-to-avoid-danger.description: May you misstate Jewish law to escape a dangerous decree or mandate? The Yam Shel Shlomo says never, as discussed in an article on Bava Kamma 60b.

honesty/keeping-a-promise-made-in-ones-h.intro: While Rav Safra was saying Shema, a customer offered a price, and Rav Safra agreed to it in his mind. The customer kept raising his offer, but afterward Rav Safra sold at the first price, because he would not break a commitment made only in his heart. The Rashbam tells this on Bava Basra 89a, and the Kitzur Shulchan Aruch says the story is for us to follow.
honesty/keeping-a-promise-made-in-ones-h.description: Must you keep a deal you only agreed to in your mind? Rav Safra kept to the first price he accepted silently, as the Rashbam relates on Bava Basra 89a.

honesty/lies-that-will-be-exposed.intro: When Ulla reported that Elul had 30 days, Rav Kahane said anyone would be believed, since people do not lie about what will soon be revealed. On Rosh Hashanah 22, the Rivash and the Sfas Emes explain the rule differently, which may matter for a boy claiming to be bar mitzvah. [On Amtrak, Alabama, and Assumptions](/daf/rosh-hashanah/22/on-amtrak-alabama-and-assumptions) asks whether it still holds in an age of brazen lies.
honesty/lies-that-will-be-exposed.description: People don't lie about facts that will soon come out, says Rav Kahane on Rosh Hashanah 22. The Rivash and Sfas Emes explain it, and does it still hold?

honesty/lying-to-a-patient-to-reassure-h.intro: Why not just tell a sick person that his request was done, and avoid any Shabbos problem? The Yad Chanoch answers that such a trick only works once. In [Message Received](/daf/bava-basra/156/message-received), the Gemara on Bava Basra 156b requires a real kinyan, and Rav Yonasan Eibeschutz says a patient who knows we might lie will never feel at ease.
honesty/lying-to-a-patient-to-reassure-h.description: Should we fool a sick person into thinking his wish was done? The Yad Chanoch and Rav Yonasan Eibeschutz say honesty works better. From Bava Basra 156b.

honesty/lying-to-an-app.intro: Is it a problem to tell Waze you are a passenger when you are really the driver, assuming no safety issue? [Lying Waze](/daf/bava-basra/82/lying-waze) starts from the Rashbam on Bava Basra 82a, which Rav Chaim Kanievsky explains through the Yerei'im: the Torah's ban on falsehood may apply only to lies that can harm someone. Still, a habit of lying, even to a computer, can train the tongue to speak falsehood.
honesty/lying-to-an-app.description: Is it wrong to tell an app you are a passenger when you are driving? The Yerei'im, Rav Chaim Kanievsky and Bava Basra 82a on lying when no one is harmed.

honesty/unpaid-items-under-the-shopping-.intro: A case of seltzer sat unnoticed under a shopping cart, and the next week the manager wondered if it was paid. Yoma 86a says Rav saw delayed payment to a butcher as a chillul Hashem, and Rashi limits that to a role model. The Ben Yehoyada says an adam gadol must stay above any suspicion, even making sure everything in his cart is marked paid.
honesty/unpaid-items-under-the-shopping-.description: Is an unmarked item under your shopping cart a problem? Rav's concern in Yoma 86a, with Rashi and the Ben Yehoyada on avoiding any hint of suspicion.

honesty/when-a-scholar-may-bend-the-trut.intro: Bava Metzia 23b says a scrupulously honest scholar may say something untrue in only three areas. He may hide who his host is so the host is not swamped with guests, he may humbly deny knowing a mesechta, and he may speak untruthfully about "puraya." The Maharsha reads that last word as Purim: the scholar claims to be drunk when he is not.
honesty/when-a-scholar-may-bend-the-trut.description: When may an honest scholar say something untrue? Bava Metzia 23b lists three cases: protecting his host, humility about learning, and Purim.

honesty/white-lies-to-spare-feelings.intro: Rebbe Yochanan HaChorani turned down a gift of olives with a simple excuse: I don't eat olives. Rav Aharon Kotler explains that this untruth was permitted so as not to offend Rebbe Tzadok, and it was not a total lie, since he meant olives moist with oil. The story, told around Yevamos 15, shows a sage who would rather go hungry than hurt someone's feelings.
honesty/white-lies-to-spare-feelings.description: May you bend the truth to spare someone's feelings? Rav Aharon Kotler on Rebbe Yochanan HaChorani's excuse for refusing olives, from Yevamos 15.

anger/getting-angry-over-spills.intro: When someone spills wine at the table, most homeowners want to yell. The Taz reads the Gemara in Eruvin 65a literally: a house where wine was spilled is blessed when the owner reacts as calmly as if it were water. Since poverty is a punishment for anger, staying calm over a spill brings blessing into the home.
anger/getting-angry-over-spills.description: Why does staying calm when wine is spilled bring blessing? The Taz explains the Gemara in Eruvin 65a: anger leads to poverty, and patience to prosperity.

anger/raising-a-hand-against-another-jew.intro: Sanhedrin 58b teaches that whoever raises his hand to hit another is called a rasha, even if he never strikes. The Shulchan Aruch codifies this, and the Rema says such a person needs a beis din to permit his cherem before he counts for a minyan. The Sma infers from the wording that he is in cherem automatically.
anger/raising-a-hand-against-another-jew.description: Even lifting a hand to hit someone makes one a rasha, says Sanhedrin 58b. The Shulchan Aruch, the Rema and the Sma on the cherem that follows.

anger/using-delays-to-build-patience.intro: Being stuck in a long line can feel like a waste of time. Rabbi Zelig Pliskin suggests seeing it instead as a chance to work on patience, since Rabbi Yisrael Salanter taught that changing a trait takes a lifetime. [One in a Million](/daf/bava-basra/145/one-in-a-million) ties this to the verse about the good-hearted having a continual feast on Bava Basra 145a, and tells of a man thrilled to change a flat tire.
anger/using-delays-to-build-patience.description: Can waiting in line become a chance to grow? Rabbi Zelig Pliskin on turning delays into practice in patience, tied to a verse on Bava Basra 145a.

lashon-hara/believing-lashon-hara-from-a.intro: The Chofetz Chaim allows a rare exception: if a listener trusts a speaker as if he were two witnesses, he may accept negative information as fact. Rav Moshe Feinstein ruled that if it later proves false, the listener is an oines. Using Rava's wife in Kesubos 85a, he explains that this trust comes not from assuming righteousness but from knowing firsthand that the speaker never lies.
lashon-hara/believing-lashon-hara-from-a.description: When may one believe lashon hara from someone who never lies, and what if it proves false? Rav Moshe Feinstein and the Chofetz Chaim, on Kesubos 85a.

lashon-hara/calling-someone-bald.intro: Is calling someone bald an insult? Rabbeinu Yitzchak suggests that Rebbe Yehoshua ben Korcha on Bava Basra 113 was Rebbe Akiva's son, with Korcha meaning the bald one. Rabbeinu Tam disagrees, proving from the youths who called Elisha HaNavi bald and were mauled by bears that the term is derogatory, so the Tanna must be the son of a man named Kerach.
lashon-hara/calling-someone-bald.description: Is it insulting to call someone bald? Rabbeinu Yitzchak and Rabbeinu Tam debate the name of Rebbe Yehoshua ben Korcha on Bava Basra 113, citing Elisha.

lashon-hara/excessive-praise-and-lashon-.intro: A Beraisa warns that a person should not speak about his friend's good qualities. How can praise be a problem? The Rashbam on Bava Basra 164b explains that heaping praise on someone invites a listener to add a "but" about his flaws, and the Maharsha and Iyun Yaakov show how even a compliment can carry a hidden criticism.
lashon-hara/excessive-praise-and-lashon-.description: How can praising someone lead to lashon hara? The Rashbam, Maharsha and Iyun Yaakov on the warning against praising a friend, from Bava Basra 164b.

lashon-hara/lashon-hara-in-front-of-thre.intro: Rabba bar Rav Huna says that anything said before three people is not lashon hara. Does that mean public gossip is allowed? On Bava Basra 39b, the Chofetz Chaim rejects the idea, citing Kesubos 11a among his proofs, and Tosfos in Arachin explains that it refers to words that could be taken either way.
lashon-hara/lashon-hara-in-front-of-thre.description: Is something said in front of three people not lashon hara? The Chofetz Chaim rejects that reading of Bava Basra 39b, with a proof from Kesubos 11a.

lashon-hara/lashon-hara-in-shidduch-refe.intro: A teacher asked about a former student for a shidduch blurted out that honesty was not her strong point, and then regretted it for weeks. Then a chosson's mother called to say that was exactly what they wanted. Rav Zilberstein, building on Menachos 64a, says her words were actually positive for that listener, so she need not do teshuvah for lashon hara.
lashon-hara/lashon-hara-in-shidduch-refe.description: A teacher's slip about a student turned out to help a shidduch. Was it lashon hara at all? Rav Zilberstein says no, reasoning from Menachos 64a.

lashon-hara/massacre-of-the-kohanim-of-n.intro: When Dovid fled, the Kohen Gadol Achimelech gave him bread and a sword, and Doeg reported it to Shaul in a way that made it sound like a conspiracy. Shaul's generals refused to kill the kohanim, but Doeg wiped out the whole city of Nov. Alongside Bava Basra 73b, the article explains who was punished, including Yehonasan, who failed to give Dovid food.
lashon-hara/massacre-of-the-kohanim-of-n.description: How did slander and a small oversight lead to the massacre of the kohanim of Nov? Doeg, Shaul and Yehonasan are held to account, alongside Bava Basra 73b.

lashon-hara/never-speaking-lashon-hara.intro: On Purim in Radin, a tipsy bachur asked the Chofetz Chaim for a promise of Gan Eden together with him. The Chofetz Chaim said that from the day he understood, he never spoke or heard lashon hara, and offered the same promise if the boy took that on. [The Spinmeisters](/daf/yoma/66/the-spinmeisters) tells this story beside Yoma 66b, and the bachur could not commit.
lashon-hara/never-speaking-lashon-hara.description: The Chofetz Chaim never spoke or heard lashon hara, and offered a bachur Gan Eden for the same pledge. Rav Sholom Schwadron's story, with Yoma 66b.

lashon-hara/not-embarrassing-someone-bei.intro: Bilam set out to curse the Jewish people, yet Rashi explains that his talking donkey died at once so no one would point at it and shame him. The same care appears on Pesachim 85b, where a person whose korban is burned in public is spared any extra shame. If the wicked are treated this way, how much more so our friends and family.
lashon-hara/not-embarrassing-someone-bei.description: Even a sinner should suffer no more shame than needed. From Bilam's donkey to the burned korban Pesach of Pesachim 85b, the Torah guards human dignity.

lashon-hara/praying-for-others-instead-o.intro: The Gemara on Pesachim 87b records that Hashem told Hoshea HaNavi that Bnei Yisrael had sinned, and Hoshea answered that they could be exchanged for another nation. Hashem rebuked him, since a father would never switch his child, and told him he should have prayed for their forgiveness instead of speaking ill of them. The Ahavas Tzion reads Hoshea's words as a call for exile, to teach a stingy generation the lesson of Bava Basra 10a.
lashon-hara/praying-for-others-instead-o.description: Hashem rebuked Hoshea HaNavi for speaking against Bnei Yisrael instead of praying for them. The lesson of Pesachim 87b on defending, not criticizing.

lashon-hara/publicizing-a-wrongdoers-act.intro: Should a person's misdeeds ever be made public? On Rosh Hashanah 26b, a robbery victim told Levi only that someone was "kava" him, and the Sifsei Chachamim says he spoke in a riddle to avoid shaming the thief. Still, the Chofetz Chaim permits exposing an unrepentant sinner in some cases so others don't follow him, a point the article draws from Yehudah's words to Yosef.
lashon-hara/publicizing-a-wrongdoers-act.description: When may you reveal someone's wrongdoing? The robbery victim's riddle on Rosh Hashanah 26b and the Chofetz Chaim's rule for warning others about a sinner.

lashon-hara/publicly-embarrassing-someon.intro: The Gemara says it is better to jump into a fiery furnace than to shame someone in public. Some Rishonim take this as an exaggeration, but Tosfos reads it literally. Discussed with Bava Kamma 60b, Tosfos explains that when someone is shamed the blood drains from his face, which is like murder, so it falls under the three cardinal sins.
lashon-hara/publicly-embarrassing-someon.description: Is it truly better to enter a furnace than to shame someone publicly? Tosfos takes it literally, likening shaming to murder. Discussed with Bava Kamma 60b.

lashon-hara/shifting-blame-by-naming-som.intro: Rebbe found a poorly written document and looked at his son with displeasure. Rebbe Shimon answered that he had not written it, R' Yehudah Chayata had, and Rebbe told him to stop speaking lashon hara. In [Bound To Get Criticized](/daf/bava-basra/164/bound-to-get-criticized), Bava Basra 164b shows that Rebbe Shimon could have cleared himself without naming who wrote it.
lashon-hara/shifting-blame-by-naming-som.description: May you clear yourself of a mistake by naming who really made it? Rebbe called it lashon hara when his son named the scribe, in Bava Basra 164b.

lashon-hara/speaking-negatively-about-th.intro: Yeshaya HaNavi said that he dwelled among people of impure lips, and Rashi notes that as rebuke this would have been fine, but here it was extraneous. The Ben Yehoyada explains that his soul departed just as the ax reached his mouth, a sign he was punished for maligning the Jewish nation without purpose. The lesson, drawn from Yevamos 49, is that even rebellious Jews keep a spark of righteousness.
lashon-hara/speaking-negatively-about-th.description: Is it wrong to criticize the Jewish people without a purpose? Yeshaya HaNavi's words, Rashi, and the Ben Yehoyada on his death, from Yevamos 49.

lashon-hara/spreading-bad-news.intro: The Shulchan Aruch applies the pasuk one who spreads gossip is a fool to someone who needlessly tells a person that a relative died. The Kitzur Shulchan Aruch writes that one should not, and a rav explained that it is foolish but not truly forbidden. The Otzros Torah wonders why people are not more careful, and the article on Moed Katan 20a sees this as a path to more careful speech.
lashon-hara/spreading-bad-news.description: Why is needlessly spreading bad news called foolish? The Shulchan Aruch, the Kitzur and the Otzros Torah on careful speech, from Moed Katan 20a.

lashon-hara/taking-blame-to-spare-anothe.intro: How far should one go to spare another person shame? [Tidy Words In A Tidy World](/daf/rosh-hashanah/26/tidy-words-in-a-tidy-world) tells of a yeshiva bachur who took the blame for his roommate's messy room, and of Rav Moshe Feinstein, who stayed silent when a driver shut the car door on his fingers. On Rosh Hashanah 26b, even a robbery victim chose his words so the thief would not be embarrassed.
lashon-hara/taking-blame-to-spare-anothe.description: A bachur took the blame for his roommate's mess; Rav Moshe Feinstein hid his pain. How far to go to avoid shaming others, from Rosh Hashanah 26b.

shalom/chassid-who-slept-in-a-cemetery.intro: Tosfos on Rosh Hashanah 16a cites the story of a pious man who gave a poor man a dinar in a famine year, angering his wife. To escape the quarrel he slept on Rosh Hashanah night in a cemetery and overheard spirits speaking of hail. [Rosh Hashana in a Cemetery](/daf/rosh-hashanah/16/rosh-hashana-in-a-cemetery) brings the Iyun Yaakov: he avoided a friend's house so no one would think badly of his wife.
shalom/chassid-who-slept-in-a-cemetery.description: Why did a pious sage sleep in a cemetery on Rosh Hashanah night? The story Tosfos cites on Rosh Hashanah 16a, and its lesson about a spouse's dignity.

shalom/confessing-to-clear-others-of-sus.intro: A tenant burned a neighbor's stroller that kept blocking the stairs, then paid for it and asked Rav Yitzchak Zilberstein if he could admit it. Rav Zilberstein said he can and possibly should, so the other tenants won't suspect one another. He learns this from Reuven in Sotah 7b, who confessed so that his brothers would not suspect each other.
shalom/confessing-to-clear-others-of-sus.description: May you admit a wrong in public so innocent neighbors aren't suspected? Rav Zilberstein learns it from Reuven's confession to his brothers in Sotah 7b.

shalom/lying-for-shalom-bayis.intro: Rav's wife always cooked the opposite of what he asked, so his son Chiya reversed the requests, and Rav told him not to lie. Yevamos 63a raises the question the Maharsha asks: isn't it permitted to change the truth for shalom bayis? The Maharsha answers that Chiya was lying every single day, and constant lying harms the soul even when the goal is peace.
shalom/lying-for-shalom-bayis.description: May you change the truth for peace at home? Rav scolded his son for it in Yevamos 63a, and the Maharsha explains that constant lying was the problem.

shalom/misjudging-others-intentions.intro: When Yosef said the bracha over his miracle at the pit, his brothers grew afraid and made up a message from Yaakov asking him to forgive them, a fabrication according to Yevamos 65a. They saw such intense joy that they assumed he was reliving the past and still bore a grudge. [She’asah Nissim](/daf/yevamos/65/sheasah-nissim) draws the lesson that even tzaddikim can misjudge each other, and knowing this can bring more shalom.
shalom/misjudging-others-intentions.description: Why did Yosef's brothers fear him after Yaakov died? A bracha said with deep feeling, a misread motive, and a lesson in shalom, from Yevamos 65a.

derech-eretz/bilams-talking-donkey.intro: Bilam set out to destroy the Jewish people, and his donkey spoke up to rebuke him. Rashi explains that the donkey died right away, because people would have pointed to it as the donkey that silenced Bilam. Alongside Rosh Hashanah 26b, the lesson is that if even a wicked man is spared needless humiliation, we must be far more careful with friends and family.
derech-eretz/bilams-talking-donkey.description: Why did Bilam's talking donkey die right after it spoke? Rashi says it spared Bilam shame, a lesson in dignity paired with Rosh Hashanah 26b's story.

derech-eretz/declining-food-without-offe.intro: How do you refuse food over a stringency without implying the host keeps a lower standard? Rebbe Yochanan HaChorani followed Beis Hillel, while Rebbe Tzadok, a talmid of Beis Shammai, was justified in following his own yeshiva's rulings. As Rav Aharon Kotler explains the story on Yevamos 15, asking outright whether the olives met Beis Hillel's standard would have been slightly disrespectful, so he declined without saying why.
derech-eretz/declining-food-without-offe.description: How can you turn down food over a kashrus concern without insulting the host? Rebbe Yochanan HaChorani and Rav Aharon Kotler's lesson, Yevamos 15.

derech-eretz/fifth-shulchan-aruch.intro: The Maggid Mishneh writes that the Torah's command to do what is just and good could not list every case, since people and their conduct change. We are expected to apply it on our own, which is often called the Fifth Shulchan Aruch. So when someone asks where it says something is assur, the answer may be that decency demands it, as the article on Nazir 45a shows.
derech-eretz/fifth-shulchan-aruch.description: What is the Fifth Shulchan Aruch? The Maggid Mishneh on doing what is just and good, even when no written rule spells it out, in an article on Nazir 45a.

derech-eretz/how-to-refer-to-a-convert.intro: Why does the Gemara say a convert who converted, rather than a gentile who converted? The Ritva on Yevamos 22a sees a moral lesson in the wording. Calling a ger a gentile who converted may cause him distress over his former life, and even when he is not present, it is improper to call something holy by a lowly name.
derech-eretz/how-to-refer-to-a-convert.description: Why shouldn't a convert be called a gentile who converted? The Ritva finds a moral lesson in the Gemara's wording on Yevamos 22a about a ger.

derech-eretz/judging-people-by-appearanc.intro: Judges in the Gemara were great tzaddikim, so why worry that fine clothes would sway them? Rav Yehuda Leib Chasman explains that even the righteous are moved by what they see, not by what they know. [Courtly Appearances](/daf/shevuos/31/courtly-appearances) brings this lesson from Shevuos 31a to Lot's sons-in-law, and to how we greet a sharp-dressed visitor and a shabby one in shul.
derech-eretz/judging-people-by-appearanc.description: Can even righteous judges be swayed by how people look? Shevuos 31a and Rav Chasman on bias, and how we greet well-dressed and shabby guests in shul.

derech-eretz/knocking-before-entering-a-.intro: After Adam sinned, Hashem first called out to him, Where are you, and the Midrash learns from this that one must knock before entering a room. Rav Alter Henoch Leibowitz drew a deeper lesson: even someone who wrecked your borrowed house deserves a knock first, because basic dignity is owed to everyone. A bachur chasing a phone-line tamperer at camp was told to approach the culprit like a mentch.
derech-eretz/knocking-before-entering-a-.description: Hashem asked Adam where are you before confronting him. Rav Alter Henoch Leibowitz's lesson on knocking first and treating even a wrongdoer with dignity.

derech-eretz/meaning-of-yasher-koach.intro: Shkoyach is a contraction of yasher koach, more correctly yeeshar kochacha, a blessing that one's strength should be true. Its earliest source is Menachos 99b, where Reish Lakish teaches that Hashem told Moshe yeeshar kochacha for breaking the Luchos. Today most people just mean job well done, and the Nesivos Shalom says that said without thought, it is a mere thanks.
derech-eretz/meaning-of-yasher-koach.description: Where does yasher koach, or shkoyach, come from and what does it mean? Hashem's words to Moshe on breaking the Luchos in Menachos 99b, and its use today.

derech-eretz/mitzvos-based-on-logic.intro: Nazir 45a says a nazir does not shave at the entrance of the Ohel Moed because that would be degrading. Rav Yosef Engel notes that this prohibition is found nowhere, it is just logical, and it carries the force of a Torah prohibition. The Chizkuni says the generation of the Flood was punished for failing to keep the mitzvos that logic demands.
derech-eretz/mitzvos-based-on-logic.description: Are we bound by duties that logic demands with no written command? Rav Yosef Engel on the nazir's shaving in Nazir 45a and the Chizkuni on the Flood.

derech-eretz/not-keeping-anxious-people-.intro: People who are worried should not be kept waiting, even for a few seconds. The Vilna Gaon explains that Mordechai sent the fastest riders with the new decree because the Jews were living in fear. Bava Basra 147a teaches the same lesson through the Kohen Gadol, who shortened his Yom Kippur prayer for the anxious crowd outside.
derech-eretz/not-keeping-anxious-people-.description: Why must we never keep worried people waiting? The Purim couriers and the Kohen Gadol's short Yom Kippur prayer teach the lesson. From Bava Basra 147a.

kavod-hatorah/calling-a-rebbe-by-his-fir.intro: A student should not call his rebbe by his given name, and the Gemara in Sanhedrin says Geichazi was punished for doing so. So how could Rav Hamnuna call his rebbe Abba? [Abba, My Dear](/daf/yevamos/57/abba-my-dear) explains how Tosfos on Yevamos 57b allow a contemporary like Shmuel to use the name, while Rashi's reading, that Abba was an honorific title, explains the students.
kavod-hatorah/calling-a-rebbe-by-his-fir.description: May a student call his rebbe by his first name? Geichazi's punishment, Rav Hamnuna, and Rashi and Tosfos on the name Abba, from Yevamos 57b.

kavod-hatorah/daas-torah.intro: Rav Huna scolded his son Rabbah for skipping Rav Chisdah's lessons, which taught life lessons instead of Gemara. Why ask a Torah scholar about matters that are not halacha? An article filed on Bava Metzia 33 lists the reasons: Torah makes a person wise, a tzaddik rises above bias, and Hashem helps those who fear Him, and Rav Henoch Leibowitz adds that the Torah itself speaks to life's dilemmas.
kavod-hatorah/daas-torah.description: Why seek a gadol's guidance on non-halachic life questions? Wisdom, freedom from bias and Divine help, plus the Torah's own view, Bava Metzia 33.

kavod-hatorah/paskening-in-front-of-your.intro: The Gemara in Eruvin 63a says Yehoshua was punished with having no children for deciding a halacha in front of Moshe Rabbeinu. When Eldad and Meidad prophesied publicly, Yehoshua told Moshe how to punish them, doing the very thing he condemned in them. The article on Pesachim 10 suggests he was so upset at the affront to his rebbe that he spoke without realizing what he was doing.
kavod-hatorah/paskening-in-front-of-your.description: Why is ruling on halacha in front of your rebbe so serious? Yehoshua's words about Eldad and Meidad, and the harsh punishment he received in Eruvin 63a.

kavod-hatorah/praising-a-dvar-torah.intro: Is calling a dvar Torah a good vort really a compliment? The Maharsha and the Ben Yehoyada say praising one teaching implies that others are not as good, so it is better to say nothing. The Rashash and the Tiferes Yisrael disagree and forbid only calling a teaching not nice, in a discussion that grows out of Eruvin 64.
kavod-hatorah/praising-a-dvar-torah.description: Does praising one dvar Torah imply others are lesser? The Maharsha, the Rashash and the Tiferes Yisrael debate the warning, in a discussion on Eruvin 64.

kavod-hatorah/serving-talmidei-chachamim.intro: Why did Rebbe Yochanan offer to carry someone's clothing to the bathhouse, rather than just study under him? In [Two Points of View](/daf/bava-metzia/41/two-points-of-view), Rebbe Aharon Levine notes that Rebbe Yochanan himself taught that serving talmidei chachamim is greater than learning from them, on Bava Metzia 41a. Rashi calls that very task too menial for an eved Ivri.
kavod-hatorah/serving-talmidei-chachamim.description: Why is serving a Torah scholar greater than learning from him? Rebbe Yochanan's offer to carry clothing shows the humility involved, Bava Metzia 41a.

kavod-hatorah/student-who-surpasses-his-.intro: Does a student who surpasses his rebbe still owe him the honor due a rebbe? The Mahari Bruna noted that in Niddah 14b, Rebbe Chiya addressed Rebbe Yehudah haNasi simply as you, without the title Rebbe. Tosfos explains that Rebbe Chiya had become a talmid chaver, his teacher's equal, even though Eruvin 92a shows Rebbe Yehudah was his main source of Torah.
kavod-hatorah/student-who-surpasses-his-.description: Must a student who becomes his rebbe's equal still give him a rebbe's honor? The Mahari Bruna and Tosfos on Rebbe Chiya in Niddah 14b and Eruvin 92a.

kavod-hatorah/torah-scholars-doing-menia.intro: Makkos 14a tells of Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi, shopping for a cow for his son's wedding. Doesn't a Torah leader lose dignity doing such tasks himself? The Pri Megadim explains that a mitzvah raises a scholar's stature, and onlookers knew the cow was for the seudas mitzvah, just as Rav Nachman built a fence around his roof with his own hands.
kavod-hatorah/torah-scholars-doing-menia.description: Does a rabbi lose dignity doing physical work for a mitzvah? The Pri Megadim explains why the Nasi bought a cow for a wedding, from Makkos 14a.

mussar/abandoning-a-plan-at-the-last-sta.intro: The Maayana Shel Torah notes that Hashem consulted the angels about man only after the rest of Creation, and Sanhedrin 39a teaches that without man the world lacks purpose. The lesson is that even at a project's last stage, one must be ready to drop it. [Words of Advice](/daf/sanhedrin/38/words-of-advice) tells how Rav Henoch Leibowitz canceled a yeshiva year in Eretz Yisrael and was ready to give up a new building.
mussar/abandoning-a-plan-at-the-last-sta.description: Hashem consulted the angels only at Creation's end. The Maayana Shel Torah and Rav Henoch Leibowitz on dropping a plan at the last stage, Sanhedrin 39a.

mussar/believing-in-someones-potential.intro: The Ritva reads Yoma 18a simply: Yehoshua ben Gamla really was an ignoramus who never learned the Yom Kippur pesukim, yet he grew into the role of Kohen Gadol and became a tzaddik. Perhaps his fiancée saw something in him he did not see himself. The man who lacked a basic education went on to make sure every Jewish child would have one, a reminder never to overlook anyone's potential.
mussar/believing-in-someones-potential.description: Can belief in someone change him? The Ritva on Yehoshua ben Gamla, who grew from an ignoramus into a tzaddik and founded schools, from Yoma 18a.

mussar/ben-sorer-umoreh-lesson.intro: The Ramban says the ben sorer umoreh broke two mitzvos: to be holy, and to cleave to Hashem. But most of us also fall short of living every moment for Hashem. In a discussion filed on Makkos 10, Rav Henoch Leibowitz explains the difference: we at least hope to reach that ideal someday, while the rebellious son has no goal beyond earthly pleasure.
mussar/ben-sorer-umoreh-lesson.description: What does the rebellious son teach about living with no spiritual goal? The Ramban and Rav Henoch Leibowitz, from an article filed on Makkos 10.

mussar/daily-mussar-study.intro: Where should someone who wants real growth begin? Rav Yisrael Salanter wrote that the foundation of spiritual growth is learning mussar every day. The Mishnah Berurah quotes the AriZal and the Vilna Gaon that daily mussar is an absolute obligation, a fitting first step in a discussion that begins with Mar Ukva in Chullin 105a.
mussar/daily-mussar-study.description: Is there an obligation to learn mussar daily? Rav Yisrael Salanter, the AriZal and the Vilna Gaon on the basis of growth, in a discussion on Chullin 105a.

mussar/eating-and-sleeping-as-serving-ha.intro: The Chofetz Chaim asks why the Malach HaMaves did not take Rav Chisda while he ate or slept. He answers that, following the Rambam, Rav Chisda ate, slept and worked only to stay healthy to serve Hashem, so even these acts were mitzvos. Tied to Makkos 10, the Chiddushei HaRim finds the same idea in Sarah Imeinu's 127 years.
mussar/eating-and-sleeping-as-serving-ha.description: Can eating, sleeping and earning a living become serving Hashem? The Chofetz Chaim, the Rambam and the story of Rav Chisda's death, tied to Makkos 10.

mussar/fear-of-public-opinion.intro: Worry about what others think can quietly push a person to give up what he knows is right. The Mishnah in Horayos 2 demands that someone who knows the Sanhedrin erred must stand up, even alone, and not hide in the crowd. In [A Standout Moment](/daf/horayos/2/a-standout-moment), this is shown to be the heart of Novardok's mission.
mussar/fear-of-public-opinion.description: How does fear of public opinion weaken a person's convictions? The Mishnah in Horayos 2 demands standing alone against the crowd, as Novardok taught.

mussar/hidden-motives-behind-our-choices.intro: Moshe could have hidden his mistake for the sake of the Torah, to protect its authority from people like Korach. The Chochmas HaMitzpun says Moshe saw that, under the noble excuse, the real motive was his own honor. The lesson drawn from Zevachim 101a is to ask whether a choice is truly right or just more comfortable for us.
mussar/hidden-motives-behind-our-choices.description: Is a choice truly right, or just more comfortable? Moshe saw past a noble excuse to hide a mistake, as the Chochmas HaMitzpun explains Zevachim 101a.

mussar/inspiration-from-everyday-events.intro: Many people say they would become tzaddikim if only they saw an open miracle. The Kli Yakar, explaining Moshe's words about Korach in Nedarim 39b, teaches otherwise. Seeing Korach swallowed alive was a one-time event no one expected to face again, but visiting a sick person reminds the visitor that the same could happen to him, so everyday events can inspire change that lasts.
mussar/inspiration-from-everyday-events.description: Why can a visit to a sick person change us more than an open miracle? The Kli Yakar on Korach and bikur cholim in Nedarim 39b gives the answer.

mussar/mocking-a-single-halacha.intro: The Midrash quotes the Mishnah in Menachos 100b about the showbread, then asks how the son of Shlomis bas Divri came to curse Hashem. He began by mocking one halacha: does a king eat nine-day-old bread? He refused to believe that the bread stayed warm and fresh, and that small joke set him on a slippery slope to spiritual ruin.
mussar/mocking-a-single-halacha.description: Can making fun of one small halacha lead to spiritual ruin? The Midrash on the man who mocked the showbread and later cursed Hashem, from Menachos 100b.

mussar/negios-and-bias-in-judgment.intro: Why did Rebbe Akiva move a garden entrance before trying to convince Rebbe Elazar ben Azariah that he should not take Maaser Rishon? [Ma’aser Motivations](/daf/yevamos/86/maaser-motivations) explains on Yevamos 86b that once the question no longer touched him personally, he could weigh it fairly. Chazal teach that negios, hidden personal interests, can cloud even a great sage's judgment, and knowing this helps us choose rightly.
mussar/negios-and-bias-in-judgment.description: How can hidden interests cloud our judgment? Rebbe Akiva's way of removing Rebbe Elazar ben Azariah's personal stake first, from Yevamos 86b.

mussar/not-judging-those-who-give-in.intro: It is easy to look down on someone who gave in to temptation and think the test was simple. The Pele Yoetz learns from the Gemara's stories of great sages who nearly failed that this attitude is wrong. Rashi on Kiddushin 81a says Rebbe Meir and Rebbe Akiva first felt that way, until they saw how close they came, so those spared such tests should thank Hashem.
mussar/not-judging-those-who-give-in.description: Why shouldn't we look down on people who give in to temptation? The Pele Yoetz learns from sages who nearly failed, citing Rashi on Kiddushin 81a.

mussar/novardok-mussar-approach.intro: Novardok students asked for cheese in hardware stores and wore their clothes inside-out. The popular view is that these were exercises in humility, but the article on Horayos 2 explains a deeper aim. Novardok saw fear of public opinion as the greatest stumbling block in avodas Hashem, and trained students to be indifferent to stares and laughter.
mussar/novardok-mussar-approach.description: Why did Novardok students act foolish in public on purpose? Not just humility but freedom from fear of others, rooted in the Mishnah in Horayos 2.

mussar/rejoicing-at-an-enemys-downfall.intro: Should we celebrate when our enemies fall? Mordechai told Haman that the warning against rejoicing applies only to Jewish enemies, so the Jews could sing Az Yashir. [Half And Half](/daf/sanhedrin/39/half-and-half) concludes that half Hallel, recalling Sanhedrin 39b, is not mourning for the Egyptians but a reminder that Hashem shows compassion for all His creations.
mussar/rejoicing-at-an-enemys-downfall.description: Is it right to rejoice when an enemy falls? Mordechai's answer to Haman, half Hallel and Hashem's compassion for all creations, from Sanhedrin 39b.

mussar/responsibility-for-unintended-con.intro: Is a person held responsible for results of his actions that he could never have foreseen? On Bava Basra 73b, Rebbi Elazar says Yisrael will be called to account for fattened geese suffering while Moshiach is delayed. [The Butterfly Effect](/daf/bava-basra/73/the-butterfly-effect) adds that Yehonasan was punished for Nov because he sent Dovid away without food, and the same holds for mitzvos.
mussar/responsibility-for-unintended-con.description: Are we accountable for results of our actions we could never foresee? Bava Basra 73b and Yehonasan's story suggest yes, for sins and mitzvos alike.

mussar/slabodka-and-human-dignity.intro: Slabodka taught that the surest way to avoid sin is to grasp Gadlus HaAdam, the greatness of man. A person who knows he is created in the image of G-d will feel that a lowly aveira is beneath him. As the article on Horayos 2 explains, Slabodka felt Novardok's methods risked eroding that dignity, and a well-dressed man in a bright blue suit showed how to keep both.
mussar/slabodka-and-human-dignity.description: How did Slabodka's focus on human greatness differ from Novardok? Gadlus HaAdam as a shield against sin, in an article on Horayos 2 and the two schools.

mussar/speaking-negatively-without-being.intro: Rashi explains that Kalev had one spirit in his heart and another in his mouth, speaking like the spies while disagreeing inside. Rav Avrohom Trop asks why that deserves praise, since people say one thing and mean another every day. He answers, in this discussion on Sotah 34b, that it is very hard to speak against something without your words changing your heart, and Kalev's love for Eretz Yisrael stayed whole.
mussar/speaking-negatively-without-being.description: Can you speak against something without it changing your heart? Rav Avrohom Trop on Kalev among the spies, in a short discussion on Sotah 34b.

mussar/torah-morality-versus-secular-eth.intro: A popular newspaper column called on readers to work on their character, not just their careers. [A G-d-Based Moral Bucket List](/daf/kesubos/77/a-g-d-based-moral-bucket-list) agrees with much of it, but notes one missing word: G-d. Morals based on human whims change over time, while Torah values are timeless, and the article turns to Kesubos 77b for a model of true humility.
mussar/torah-morality-versus-secular-eth.description: Why do Torah values stay fixed while human ethics keep shifting? A popular moral bucket list column meets a model of humility from Kesubos 77b.

mussar/value-of-time.intro: In Gittin 47a, Reish Lakish left saffron to his children and was upset about it. He realized he had spent precious moments earning money for something he did not need in the end. Rav Kahaneman taught that the Chofetz Chaim lived a long life not because of his ninety-plus years, but because he used every minute of them.
mussar/value-of-time.description: Why did Reish Lakish lament leaving saffron to his children? Gittin 47a teaches that time is life, as Rav Kahaneman and the Chofetz Chaim showed.

kiddush-hashem/arguments-that-cause-chil.intro: Yehoshua was rightly upset at Eldad and Meidad, yet in defending Moshe he committed the same offense, as the Gemara in Eruvin 63a describes. The article on Pesachim 10 sees a warning here: an argument may be for the sake of heaven, but the way it is made public can become a chillul Hashem. Before taking a stand, one should check that his actions match his intentions, a bedikah of his own.
kiddush-hashem/arguments-that-cause-chil.description: How can a dispute for the sake of heaven turn into chillul Hashem? A lesson from Yehoshua in Eruvin 63a and the search for chametz in Pesachim 10.

kiddush-hashem/avoiding-suspicion.intro: Rav said in Yoma 86a that if he did not pay the butcher right away, it would be a chillul Hashem. [Shopping Cart Considerations](/daf/yoma/86/shopping-cart-considerations) shows that people in leadership are held to a higher bar. Rashi says this is because others learn from Rav. The Chasam Sofer adds that a rav must not even seem to take free meat in return for a lenient ruling.
kiddush-hashem/avoiding-suspicion.description: Why must leaders avoid even the look of wrongdoing? Rav's words in Yoma 86a, explained by Rashi, the Ben Yehoyada and the Chasam Sofer, on suspicion.

kiddush-hashem/avoiding-the-appearance-o.intro: Tosfos offers one more view of why Mordechai would not bow to Haman: he could have, but chose not to, to make a Kiddush Hashem. The article on Sanhedrin 61b compares two brothers who could have drunk water from red glasses to fool their captors, but chose death over seeming to drink forbidden wine. Rava in Megillah notes that many Jews complained Mordechai was provoking Haman needlessly.
kiddush-hashem/avoiding-the-appearance-o.description: Mordechai may have refused to bow to Haman as a Kiddush Hashem, avoiding even the look of idolatry. Tosfos, two brothers and the wine, with Sanhedrin 61b.

kiddush-hashem/paying-a-bill-promptly.intro: Rav taught that delaying payment to a butcher would be a chillul Hashem for someone like him. Rashi explains that the butcher might think Rav never meant to pay, even if he was only waiting a few days. The Chasam Sofer notes that in Yoma 86a Rav spoke of meat, since late payment could look like free meat given for a kashrus ruling.
kiddush-hashem/paying-a-bill-promptly.description: Why did Rav say paying the butcher late would be a chillul Hashem? Rashi and the Chasam Sofer explain the danger of delayed payment, from Yoma 86a.

kiddush-hashem/posing-as-a-non-jew-to-su.intro: With ships in the Red Sea claiming to be Muslim to avoid Houthi attacks, may a Jew let others think he is not Jewish to save his life? On Avodah Zarah 18b, Rebbe Meir dipped one finger in non-kosher food and sucked another, so onlookers assumed he could not be the famous rabbi. The Shulchan Aruch allows creating such an impression but forbids openly declaring another faith, and Rabbi Ephraim Oshry applied this to a soldier's identification tag.
kiddush-hashem/posing-as-a-non-jew-to-su.description: May a Jew in danger let others think he is not Jewish? Rebbe Meir's escape on Avodah Zarah 18b and the line between an impression and an open denial.

kiddush-hashem/reward-for-unintended-kid.intro: Gittin 57b says descendants of Haman, Sisera and Sancheriv became teachers of Torah. Why would such enemies of Klal Yisrael merit such descendants? Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky explains that each one caused a great kiddush Hashem without meaning to, and Hashem does not withhold any reward, even for an unwanted result.
kiddush-hashem/reward-for-unintended-kid.description: Why did Haman, Sisera and Sancheriv merit Torah scholars as descendants? Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky says they caused a kiddush Hashem, as told in Gittin 57b.

kiddush-hashem/the-ten-martyrs.intro: The Ten Martyrs, recalled in the Yom Kippur Mussaf, were great tzaddikim killed by Rome, and their deaths atone for Klal Yisrael. Rav Yaakov Emden holds they did not all live at the same time, and he proves it from a Gemara in Menachos 18a. Sanhedrin 14a tells of one of them, Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava, who was killed with 300 spears after ordaining his students.
kiddush-hashem/the-ten-martyrs.description: Did the Ten Martyrs of the Yom Kippur service all live at once? Rav Yaakov Emden says no, citing Menachos 18a, and Sanhedrin 14a tells of one of them.

kiddush-hashem/yosef-meshisa-story.intro: When the Romans feared to enter the Beis HaMikdash, they let a Jew go in first and keep what he took. Yosef Meshisa brought out the Menorah, but when sent back a second time, he refused, asking whether angering Hashem once was not enough, and died al kiddush Hashem. In [Love Thy Neighbor](/daf/kesubos/37/love-thy-neighbor), on Kesubos 37b, he shows that even a traitor keeps a hidden spark.
kiddush-hashem/yosef-meshisa-story.description: How did a collaborator who looted the Beis HaMikdash for Rome refuse a second time and die al kiddush Hashem? Yosef Meshisa's story, from Kesubos 37b.

leadership/choosing-a-rosh-yeshiva.intro: Who should lead a yeshiva: the scholar with the widest knowledge, or the one with the sharpest mind? Rav Yosef knew more Torah, while Rabba's sheer genius was beyond compare. Since most of Torah was still oral in those days, the rabbis preferred encyclopedic knowledge, in a story that grows out of a long debate in Bava Kamma 67b.
leadership/choosing-a-rosh-yeshiva.description: Broad knowledge or sharp genius? The rabbis weighed Rav Yosef against Rabba when picking a Rosh HaYeshiva, in a story tied to Bava Kamma 67b.

leadership/famine-in-the-days-of-dovid-h.intro: During a three-year famine, Dovid HaMelech checked whether the people were guilty of idolatry, immorality or unpaid charity pledges, and found them clear. The Urim v'Tumim revealed two other causes on Yevamos 78b: Shaul had not been eulogized properly, and he bore blame for the Givonim who suffered after Nov was destroyed. Rashi and the Maharsha read the Givonim's loss differently, and the Aruch L'Ner offers a third view.
leadership/famine-in-the-days-of-dovid-h.description: Why was there a famine in the days of Dovid HaMelech? Shaul's missing eulogy and the Givonim who suffered after Nov fell, as told in Yevamos 78b.

jealousy/overcoming-jealousy-of-others-s.intro: A kohen who served on a busy, sunny day felt cheated when a kohen on a rainy day brought more communal olos and kept more hides. HaRav Henoch Leibowitz taught that the root of jealousy is the feeling that someone took what was ours. Chizkiya in Shekalim 6 explains that a separate box for each day showed the kohanim plainly that no one had touched their share.
jealousy/overcoming-jealousy-of-others-s.description: How do you stop feeling that someone else's gain is your loss? The six collection boxes of Shekalim 6 and HaRav Henoch Leibowitz on the root of jealousy.

ahavas-yisrael/dignity-for-the-condemned.intro: Even a man condemned to death keeps his dignity. The righteous women of Yerushalayim brought him a drink of levonah to dull the pain, and beis din supplied it if they did not. For sereifah, the Gemara chooses the method that leaves the body intact, fulfilling "Love thy neighbor," as the article on Sanhedrin 44 explains.
ahavas-yisrael/dignity-for-the-condemned.description: Love your neighbor applies to the condemned: a drink to dull the pain and a dignified death. The Torah's compassion in capital cases, Sanhedrin 44.

ahavas-yisrael/kol-yisrael-areivim-zeh-l.intro: Kol Yisrael areivim zeh la'zeh: Jews are held responsible for each other's sins when they could have prevented them. Avodah Zarah 18 shows how far this goes, since even a righteous person can be accountable for others. That burden becomes a call to reach out, whether through a Shabbos invitation, mishloach manos to an unaffiliated Jew, a study partnership, or simply a sincere and warm greeting.
ahavas-yisrael/kol-yisrael-areivim-zeh-l.description: All Jews are responsible for one another. How the Gemara on Avodah Zarah 18 turns that idea into a call for outreach, from Shabbos meals to warm greetings.

ahavas-yisrael/loving-a-wicked-person.intro: Does the mitzvah to love your fellow include a sinner? The Hagahos Maimonis limits it to one who keeps Torah and mitzvos, and the Rambam calls for hating an unrepentant sinner, yet Kesubos 37b applies the verse to a condemned man. The Baal HaTanya explains that one hates the evil deeds while loving the spark of G-dliness that every Jew carries.
ahavas-yisrael/loving-a-wicked-person.description: Does love your fellow as yourself include a wicked person? The Hagahos Maimonis, the Ramah and the Baal HaTanya, based on Kesubos 37b and Sanhedrin 52b.

ahavas-yisrael/seeing-potential-in-every.intro: Avraham Avinu ran to serve three idol worshippers, seeing in each a spark of G-dliness, because every person is made b'tzelem Elokim. Yet in the Gemara on Menachos 53, he seemed to think Klal Yisrael was beyond hope, until Hashem compared them to a slow-growing olive tree. [It’s Never Too Late](/daf/menachos/53/its-never-too-late) draws the lesson for kiruv: no Jew is ever too far gone.
ahavas-yisrael/seeing-potential-in-every.description: Can any Jew be too far gone? Avraham saw a spark in every guest, and Hashem's olive tree answer teaches the potential in each Jew, from Menachos 53.

simchah/tu-bav.intro: The last Mishnah in Taanis names Tu B'Av and Yom Kippur as the most joyous days of the year, and Taanis 30b asks what made the Fifteenth of Av special. [Who Knows Fifteen?](/daf/taanis/30/who-knows-fifteen) walks through the answers, which the Rashbam says do not argue: the end of marriage limits between shevatim, the burial of Beitar's victims, and the end of the decree on the generation of the spies.
simchah/tu-bav.description: Why was Tu B'Av among the most joyous days of the year? Marriages between shevatim, Beitar's burial, and the spies' generation, from Taanis 30b.

tochachah/protesting-public-embarrassmen.intro: The Midrash says Rabbi Zecharia ben Avkolos was at the party when Bar Kamtza was thrown out, and he could have protested but did not. The Eitz Yosef explains that rebuking the host would have felt arrogant, and he may have thought others would speak up. Yet the Midrash singles him out, which suggests only his words would have helped, as the article on Gittin 55b explains.
tochachah/protesting-public-embarrassmen.description: Must a respected person speak up when someone is shamed in public? Rabbi Zecharia ben Avkolos stayed silent at Bar Kamtza's ejection, from Gittin 55b.

tochachah/responsibility-to-protest-wron.intro: On Avodah Zarah 18 the Gemara declares that anyone who can protest and does not will be punished on account of the sinner. That is why Rabi Chanina ben Tradyon's wife suffered: Rashi says she should have told her husband not to pronounce the Ineffable Name, while the Chasam Sofer says she should have guided her daughter in tzniyus. The Maharsha explains her dying words as accepting that failing to correct others was reason enough.
tochachah/responsibility-to-protest-wron.description: Is one who could protest a sin and stays silent held responsible? The wife of Rabi Chanina ben Tradyon on Avodah Zarah 18, with Rashi and the Chasam Sofer.

yetzer-hara/needing-heavenly-help-agains.intro: The Mesillas Yesharim writes that a person cannot beat his yetzer hara without Heavenly help, though he must still do his part first. The ba'alei mussar ask why Hashem made it so, and answer that He wants us to depend on Him and build a relationship. The article on Sanhedrin 2 pairs this with the Satmar Rebbe's point about needing help to reach the right halacha.
yetzer-hara/needing-heavenly-help-agains.description: Why can't we beat the yetzer hara on our own? The Mesillas Yesharim and the ba'alei mussar on effort, Divine help and relying on Hashem, with Sanhedrin 2.

yetzer-hara/spiritual-struggles-and-setb.intro: In Yoma 66b, Rebbe Eliezer answers a wise woman by pointing to women who spun wool while it was still on the sheep, a skill hidden in the final thread. The lesson is to value the process, not just the result. Rav Hutner wrote the same to a discouraged student: we see the greatness of the Chofetz Chaim but not his battles, so lose battles but win wars.
yetzer-hara/spiritual-struggles-and-setb.description: Why setbacks should not crush someone trying to grow: Rav Hutner's letter on the hidden struggles of great people, with Rebbe Eliezer in Yoma 66b.

yetzer-hara/tzaddikim-struggling-with-te.intro: Kiddushin 39b and 81a tell of great sages tested by temptation. Some escaped through miracles, Rav Amram Chasida stopped himself by shouting that his house was on fire, and Rebbe Chiya bar Ashi believed he had sinned. In [Moral Of The Story](/daf/kiddushin/81/moral-of-the-story), the Divrei Shaul explains that these stories show tzaddikim face the same yetzer hara we do, so their victories can inspire us.
yetzer-hara/tzaddikim-struggling-with-te.description: Did great sages face the same desires as everyone? The Divrei Shaul on the stories of tzaddikim tested by temptation in Kiddushin 39b and 81a.

emunah-and-bitachon/bitachon-versus-tefi.intro: Once something has already happened, it is too late for tefillah. The Meiri, often quoted by Rabbi Shaya Cohen, says it is not too late for bitachon. Learning from Hillel in Berachos 60a, a tzaddik who hears a commotion can trust that it is not in his house, because bitachon, unlike tefillah, is not limited to the ways of nature.
emunah-and-bitachon/bitachon-versus-tefi.description: When it is too late to pray, is it too late to trust Hashem? The Meiri says bitachon reaches where tefillah cannot, from Hillel's story in Berachos 60a.

emunah-and-bitachon/family-time-versus-c.intro: People who run shuls, schools and chesed groups can find these projects swallowing all their time. Rav Henoch Leibowitz taught that if Hashem wants a school to stay open, it will, even without someone fundraising until midnight every night. A person should do his best in the time available, leave time for family, and leave the rest to Hashem, a lesson drawn from Yeshaya's words to Chizkiya on Yevamos 49b.
emunah-and-bitachon/family-time-versus-c.description: Should communal work come before family time? Rav Henoch Leibowitz on doing your best and leaving the rest to Hashem, a lesson from Yevamos 49b.

emunah-and-bitachon/finding-the-positive.intro: The Netziv was poor, yet he told the wealthy Rashash that toiling to learn in hard circumstances was exactly what made him greater in Torah. Alongside Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya's answer in Nedarim 50b, the article shows how each hardship carries a hidden tradeoff. Rabbi Zelig Pliskin's audience even met a man who thanked Hashem for a flat tire, since it proved he could lift heavy things after surgery.
emunah-and-bitachon/finding-the-positive.description: How can poverty or loss hide a benefit? The Netziv, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and a flat tire show how to focus on the positive. Nedarim 50b.

emunah-and-bitachon/hidden-providence-in.intro: Rome will claim its marketplaces, bathhouses and wealth were all for the Jews, and on Avodah Zarah 2 Hashem calls them fools. The Chiddushei HaGriz explains that Rome is not lying, only foolish: from the Divine view, their deeds really did serve Torah, even though that was never their intent. Other nations can be unwitting instruments of Providence, and history will one day make that plain.
emunah-and-bitachon/hidden-providence-in.description: Can the deeds of other nations end up serving Torah without their intent? The Chiddushei HaGriz on Rome's claims in Avodah Zarah 2 and hidden Providence.

emunah-and-bitachon/interpreting-signs-f.intro: The Yad Paltiel says the Gemara in Gittin 3b used the past tense so no one would think a found get with his own names was a sign from Heaven to divorce. In [Down In The Dumps](/daf/gittin/3/down-in-the-dumps), a story of the Brisker Rav at a wedding shows how hard such signs are to read. Rav Henoch Leibowitz warned against reading events as Divine signals, and the Vilna Gaon points to tefillah instead.
emunah-and-bitachon/interpreting-signs-f.description: Should we read events as signs from Heaven? The Yad Paltiel on a found get in Gittin 3b, the Brisker Rav, and the Vilna Gaon's advice to turn to tefillah.

emunah-and-bitachon/not-leaving-food-for.intro: The Zohar, quoted by the Mishnah Berurah, advises not to cook or save food for the next day, so that one's prayers for food are more urgent. Yet Menachos 103b reads buying food day by day as part of the tochachah, a curse. Rav Chaim Shmulevitz explains that the same empty kitchen is a blessing for one who builds trust in Hashem and a curse for one who only worries.
emunah-and-bitachon/not-leaving-food-for.description: Is buying food day by day a blessing or a curse? The Zohar's advice, the curse in Menachos 103b, and Rav Chaim Shmulevitz on true bitachon in Hashem.

emunah-and-bitachon/shabbos-spending-rep.intro: Chazal teach that money spent honoring Shabbos and Yom Tov is not taken from a person's yearly income. In [A Sea-rious Story](/daf/bava-basra/166/a-sea-rious-story), filed on Bava Basra 166a, the Tzemach Tzedek agrees, yet he still bans overpriced fish for the sake of the poor, who cannot lay out money now. R' Reuven Feinstein adds that a Shabbos food that turns expensive may still be bought.
emunah-and-bitachon/shabbos-spending-rep.description: Is cash spent on Shabbos food repaid from Heaven, even if prices soar? The Tzemach Tzedek and R' Reuven Feinstein on the teaching, tied to Bava Basra 166a.

emunah-and-bitachon/valuing-every-posses.intro: Why did Yaakov Avinu risk going back for small jugs of little value? The Arizal explains that he knew every item Hashem gave him had a purpose in Hashem's plan, so the jugs were as precious as gold. The article on Shevuos 9a adds a friend's lesson from a cooking show: whatever Hashem puts in your bag is what you need, so make a plan with it.
emunah-and-bitachon/valuing-every-posses.description: Every possession Hashem gives has a purpose. The Arizal on why Yaakov went back for small jugs, and what Korach missed, in an article on Shevuos 9a.

emunah-and-bitachon/why-the-manna-fell-d.intro: Why did the manna fall every day instead of once a year? Rebbe Shimon bar Yochai answered with a king who gave his son a yearly allowance and saw him only once a year, so he switched to a daily one. A father in the desert worried about tomorrow and prayed each day, a theme the article builds from Chullin 60b.
emunah-and-bitachon/why-the-manna-fell-d.description: Why did the manna fall every day and not once a year? Rebbe Shimon bar Yochai's parable of a king and his son's allowance, building on Chullin 60b.

miracles/hidden-miracles-of-purim.intro: Hallel is said for open miracles, but the miracles of Purim were hidden. One could read the story like a good book without seeing Hashem's hand. Rabbi Yechezkel Roter explains Megillah 14a this way: we read the Megillah publicly from the bima with brachos to declare that Hashem was behind every seemingly natural event, so the Megillah and Hallel are not interchangeable.
miracles/hidden-miracles-of-purim.description: How do the hidden miracles of Purim differ from the open miracles of Hallel? Reading the Megillah declares Hashem's hand, as explained on Megillah 14a.

miracles/miracle-of-the-ner-maaravi.intro: The Ritva writes that every cup of the Menorah got half a log of oil and burned out by morning, except the Ner Ma'aravi, which stayed lit all day until more oil was added at evening. This daily miracle offers an answer to the Beis Yosef's question about eight days of Chanukah: the first day had a miracle too. The article builds on the Mishnah's half log in Menachos 88.
miracles/miracle-of-the-ner-maaravi.description: How did the Ner Ma'aravi burn far longer than its oil allowed? The Ritva's daily miracle answers the Beis Yosef's Chanukah question, from Menachos 88.

miracles/miracles-for-ordinary-people.intro: Can an ordinary person merit a miracle? Bava Metzia 106 asks whether the owner of a flock can claim a miracle would have saved his sheep, as one saved Dovid HaMelech. Tosfos says that through prayer, even ordinary people can merit miracles, and the article asks why Dovid did not get the greater miracle of Rebbe Chanina ben Dosa's goat.
miracles/miracles-for-ordinary-people.description: Can ordinary people merit miracles through prayer? Tosfos says yes, and a shepherd's case asks whether a possible miracle counts, in Bava Metzia 106.

miracles/miracles-for-resisting-sin.intro: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappi fled a noblewoman into a dangerous building and walked out unharmed the next morning. The rabbis cited a beraisa: one who holds back from sin when he could have sinned is granted a miracle. Kiddushin 39b adds Rabbi Tzadok, who climbed into an oven, and Rabbi Kahana, who leaped from a roof and was caught by Eliyahu.
miracles/miracles-for-resisting-sin.description: Is a person who withstands a strong temptation granted a miracle in return? Rabbi Chanina bar Pappi, Rabbi Tzadok and Rabbi Kahana in Kiddushin 39b.

miracles/nakdimon-ben-gurion-rain-miracl.intro: Nakdimon ben Gurion borrowed twelve wells of water for the pilgrims and promised to repay them or pay twelve talents of silver. When he prayed in the Beis HaMikdash, rain filled the wells, and a second prayer made the sun shine again. The Ra'avad says the sun had never set, but the Gevuras Ari says it had, and this miracle helps explain the Maharsha on Kesubos 66b.
miracles/nakdimon-ben-gurion-rain-miracl.description: Nakdimon ben Gurion prayed for rain and for the sun to shine again. Did the sun truly set? The Ra'avad and Gevuras Ari differ, tied to Kesubos 66b.

miracles/nature-as-a-hidden-miracle.intro: The Maharsha asks why, in Sotah 46b, Hashem would create a forest along with the bears that attacked the youths who mocked Elisha. The Steipler explains that they failed to see that their livelihood was a miracle hidden inside nature, which is itself a miracle. So they were punished with a miracle within a miracle: bears, and a forest for them to come from.
miracles/nature-as-a-hidden-miracle.description: Nature is as much Hashem's doing as an open miracle. The Steipler explains the bears and the forest of Sotah 46b as a miracle within a miracle.

miracles/sundial-moving-back-for-chizkiy.intro: On the day the wicked King Achaz died, Hashem cut the day short to just two hours, so there was no time to eulogize him. Years later, when Chizkiyahu recovered, the shadow on the sundial moved back ten hours and paid back the missing time. [One Small Half-Step](/daf/sanhedrin/96/one-small-half-step) traces how this long day in Sanhedrin 96 caught the eye of a king in Babylonia.
miracles/sundial-moving-back-for-chizkiy.description: The shadow on the sundial went back ten hours as a sign of Chizkiyahu's recovery, making up for Achaz's shortened day. The miracle story in Sanhedrin 96.

miracles/the-ram-at-the-akeidah.intro: Pirkei Avos suggests that the ram offered in place of Yitzchak was created in the Six Days of Creation. The Bartenura and the Meiri explain that only the decree was set then, while Rashi says the Satan trapped the ram in the thicket to hold Avraham back. Rav Henoch Leibowitz explains why that delay mattered, in a discussion connected to Sukkah 44a: inspiration fades with every passing second.
miracles/the-ram-at-the-akeidah.description: Was the Akeidah ram created at the start of time, and why was it caught in the thicket? The Meiri, Rashi and Rav Henoch Leibowitz, tied to Sukkah 44a.

miracles/wheat-that-rained-from-the-sky.intro: Menachos 69b tells of an Arab merchant named Adi on whom wheat rained down, a handbreadth deep over a vast area, and asks if such wheat could be used for the Shtei HaLechem. In [It’s Raining Wheat](/daf/menachos/69/its-raining-wheat), Tosafos says the Gemara means a miracle. The article links this to Rav Chaim Brisker's famous question about miraculous Chanukah oil.
miracles/wheat-that-rained-from-the-sky.description: Could wheat that rained from the clouds be used for a Temple offering? Menachos 69b, Tosafos on miracles and the question of miraculous Chanukah oil.

olam-haba/do-the-dead-know-what-happens-.intro: Rebbe Chiya warned that the departed might say of tzitzis dragged over their graves that tomorrow the living will join them, and now they mock them. That remark opens a long discussion in Berachos 18 about whether those already in the next world know what happens in this one.
olam-haba/do-the-dead-know-what-happens-.description: Do people who have passed away know what happens in this world? The Gemara's long discussion begins with tzitzis dragged over graves. Berachos 18.

olam-haba/kings-with-no-share-in-olam-ha.intro: The Mishnah on Sanhedrin 102b lists three kings with no share in the World to Come: Yeravam, Achav and Menashe. When Rav Ashi called them our friends, Menashe challenged him in a dream. [Breaking Bread](/daf/sanhedrin/102/breaking-bread) brings Rebbe Yehuda's view, accepted by Rebbe Yochanan, that Menashe's teshuvah earned him a portion after all.
olam-haba/kings-with-no-share-in-olam-ha.description: Which kings lose their share in Olam Haba? The Mishnah in Sanhedrin 102b names Yeravam, Achav and Menashe, but Menashe's teshuvah may have earned a place.

olam-haba/martyrs-in-olam-haba.intro: On Bava Basra 10b, Yosef the son of Rebbe Yehoshua glimpsed the World to Come and heard that no one can stand in the section of those executed by the government. The Gemara decides this means the martyrs of Lod, whom Rashi identifies as the brothers Luleyanus and Pappas, who falsely confessed to the murder of Trajan's daughter to save the community. The Mishareis Moshe explains that even people of lesser stature reach this height through such self-sacrifice.
olam-haba/martyrs-in-olam-haba.description: Who holds a place in Olam Haba that even tzaddikim cannot enter? The martyrs of Lod, Luleyanus and Pappas, who died to save the Jews, on Bava Basra 10b.

olam-haba/selling-your-share-in-olam-hab.intro: Someone once put his share in Olam Haba up for auction on eBay, and the bids reached $100,000. The Gemara in Sotah 21a and the ruling of the Rema show that such a sale is void. Rabbeinu Yerucham says trying to sell it may cost the seller his reward, while the Maharit says a buyer who paid so much for Olam Haba deserves reward.
olam-haba/selling-your-share-in-olam-hab.description: Can you sell your share in the World to Come? Sotah 21a and the Rema say no, and Rabbeinu Yerucham warns the seller may even lose his reward.

moshiach-and-geulah/birth-pangs-of-moshi.intro: Rabbah feared the pain that will come before Mashiach, and Abaye reminded him that Rebbe Eliezer says Torah and chesed protect a person from it. Rabbah answered that his sins might still leave him exposed. Rabbeinu Elchanan in Tosfos sets this against Yevamos 105a, which implies Rabbah did less chesed than Abaye, and concludes that Rabbah did kindness, just not at Abaye's level.
moshiach-and-geulah/birth-pangs-of-moshi.description: What protects a person from the birth pangs of Mashiach? Rebbe Eliezer says Torah and chesed, as Abaye told Rabbah, in a look tied to Yevamos 105a.

moshiach-and-geulah/nations-claiming-rew.intro: After Mashiach comes, Hashem will hold up a Torah and invite those who occupied themselves with it to collect their reward, and Avodah Zarah 2 describes the nations rushing in. Rome claims its markets, bathhouses and silver and gold were all for the sake of Torah, and the Raavad explains the money as sparing scholars from taxes. Hashem calls them fools, and the Chiddushei HaGriz notes that He does not call them liars.
moshiach-and-geulah/nations-claiming-rew.description: After Mashiach comes, Rome will claim reward for its markets, bathhouses and gold. Why Hashem calls the nations fools, but not liars, on Avodah Zarah 2.

moshiach-and-geulah/prayer-to-bring-mosh.intro: Rebbe asked Eliyahu HaNavi which tzaddikim could bring Moshiach by praying together, and was told: Rebbe Chiya and his sons. When they prayed on a fast day, wind blew and rain fell, but a fiery bear interrupted them before they reached the words about reviving the dead. The Brisker Rav, discussed with Bava Metzia 106, learns that even the loftiest goal does not override halacha.
moshiach-and-geulah/prayer-to-bring-mosh.description: Rebbe Chiya and his sons nearly brought Moshiach with one prayer. The Brisker Rav learns that no goal overrides halacha, in an article on Bava Metzia 106.

moshiach-and-geulah/sin-delaying-moshiac.intro: Rabbah bar Bar Chanah saw geese so fat that rivers of oil flowed beneath them, and Rebbi Elazar said Yisrael would have to give an accounting for this. The Rashbam on Bava Basra 73b explains that sins delay Moshiach, and meanwhile the geese suffer. The Ritva reads the geese as nations who will repent only when Moshiach comes.
moshiach-and-geulah/sin-delaying-moshiac.description: Do our sins delay Moshiach, and are we accountable for the suffering it causes? The Rashbam and Ritva explain Rebbi Elazar's words in Bava Basra 73b.

moshiach-and-geulah/third-beis-hamikdash.intro: Bava Kamma 60b says Hashem burned Zion with fire and will rebuild it with fire, words repeated in the Nachem prayer on Tishah B'Av. The Arugas HaBosem explains that a fire counts as having burned everything from the moment it is lit. In the same way, Hashem counts our sincere resolutions to do good as if they were already done, and that may be enough to merit the rebuilding.
moshiach-and-geulah/third-beis-hamikdash.description: Why will the third Beis HaMikdash be built with fire? The Arugas HaBosem's lesson about sincere resolutions, from the words of Bava Kamma 60b.

moshiach-and-geulah/valley-of-dry-bones.intro: Yechezkel saw dry bones come back to life, a sign that Klal Yisrael is never far from redemption. Sanhedrin 92b debates whether they lived only briefly or a full second life. Targum Yonasan says they were men of Ephraim who left Egypt thirty years too early, and Hashem led Bnei Yisrael away from the Philistines so they would not see their bodies.
moshiach-and-geulah/valley-of-dry-bones.description: Who were the dry bones Yechezkel saw revived? Men of Ephraim who left Egypt too early, says the Targum, and Sanhedrin 92b debates how long they lived.

moshiach-and-geulah/will-pork-be-permitt.intro: A Midrash says the chazir is so named because Hashem will return it to us in the future. The Toras HaMincha takes this literally, while the Minchas Kenaos says only the reason for the ban will return. In [Kosher Pork: When Pigs Fly—or When Moshiach Comes?](/daf/bechoros/27/kosher-pork-when-pigs-fly-or-when-moshiach-comes), filed on Bechoros 27, the Chasam Sofer says pigs will start chewing their cud.
moshiach-and-geulah/will-pork-be-permitt.description: Will pork be permitted when Moshiach comes? The Toras HaMincha, Minchas Kenaos and Chasam Sofer read the Midrash differently, with Bechoros 27.

tzaddikim/divine-protection-of-tzaddikim.intro: If Hashem kept the donkey of R' Pinchas ben Yair from eating untithed grain, says Chullin 7a, He surely keeps the righteous themselves from sin. Tosfos limits this protection mainly to forbidden foods. In [The Pious Donkey, the Muzzled Camels, and the Elephant in the Room](/daf/chullin/7/the-pious-donkey-the-muzzled-camels-and-the-elephant-in-the-room), this clashes with the Maharsha's view of an ordinary donkey.
tzaddikim/divine-protection-of-tzaddikim.description: Does Hashem keep tzaddikim, and even their animals, from sin? Chullin 7a, Tosfos's limit to forbidden foods, and the donkey of R' Pinchas ben Yair.

tzaddikim/rainbow-and-the-merit-of-tzadd.intro: In Kesubos 77b, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi whether a rainbow ever appeared in his lifetime. A rainbow recalls Hashem's promise after the Flood, but a great tzaddik can protect the world by his own merit. Rebbe Yehonoson Eibshitz says this was some other rainbow-like sign, while the Rema says the ordinary rainbow vanished, showing nature was suspended and still no flood came.
tzaddikim/rainbow-and-the-merit-of-tzadd.description: Why was no rainbow seen in the lifetime of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai? The Rema and Rebbe Yehonoson Eibshitz explain the meaning of the sign in Kesubos 77b.

dreams/halachic-weight-of-dreams.intro: The Maharam Mi'Rottenberg wrote that a new way to explain Kiddushin 17a came to him in a dream: whoever holds the money keeps it when a worker falls sick. The Shach was not impressed, saying dreams carry little halachic value. He also argued that the Gemara never mentions any doubt, so the rule about leaving money where it is does not apply, and Tosfos is preferred.
dreams/halachic-weight-of-dreams.description: Does a ruling revealed in a dream carry halachic weight? The Shach rejects the Maharam's dream about a sick eved Ivri and a worker, from Kiddushin 17a.

segulos/changing-a-name-as-a-segulah.intro: A kollel yungerman became very sick, and when he went to the Steipler it emerged that his wife had the same name as his mother. The Steipler urged her to change her name, and her husband fully recovered. Rav Moshe Shternbuch writes that anyone may use this solution in case of need, as the article on Menachos 29b relates.
segulos/changing-a-name-as-a-segulah.description: Can changing a name protect against danger? The Steipler told a wife sharing her mother-in-law's name to change it, as told in an article on Menachos 29b.

segulos/eliezers-sign-at-the-well.intro: Eliezer chose Rivkah by a sign, which the Gemara in Chullin 95a lists as a classic case of nichush. Tosfos says he must have asked her family first and the Torah tells it out of order. Rashi keeps the literal sequence, and the Gur Aryeh explains that Eliezer gave the bracelets at once so as not to break his moment of inspiration.
segulos/eliezers-sign-at-the-well.description: How could Eliezer rely on a sign to choose Rivkah if it is nichush? Tosfos, Rashi and the Gur Aryeh on the bracelets and the order of events, Chullin 95a.

segulos/havdalah-on-wine-segulah-for-chi.intro: The Gemara says reciting Havdalah over wine is a segulah to have boys, and Rav Chaim Kanievsky advised childless couples to use wine and not grape juice. Why do some who are careful still not have children? He gave two answers: sins may block the blessing, as the Mishna Berura writes, or the mitzvah turns what a person lacks into a source of atonement.
segulos/havdalah-on-wine-segulah-for-chi.description: Why Rav Chaim Kanievsky told childless couples to make Havdalah on wine, not grape juice, and his two answers for why segulos do not always work.

segulos/ketores-parchment-segulah.intro: A growing custom is to read the parashah of Ketores every day from a parchment written in ksav ashuris, said by some to be a segulah for wealth. The Tashbetz holds the ban on writing pesukim applies only to ksav ashuris, but he also accepts the heter of eis la'asos for reading and learning, so he would permit it. The question grows out of the golden tablet of Yoma 37a.
segulos/ketores-parchment-segulah.description: Is it proper to read Ketores daily from a handwritten parchment as a segulah for wealth? The Tashbetz on writing pesukim, in a look at Yoma 37a.

segulos/nichush-and-forbidden-divination.intro: The Torah forbids nichush, relying on omens to decide what to do. In Chullin 95a the Gemara asks whether Rav did this when he took a waiting ferry as a good sign, and it names Eliezer and Yonasan as the classic examples. Tosfos explains that Yonasan meant to attack anyway and only wanted to strengthen his armor-bearer's courage.
segulos/nichush-and-forbidden-divination.description: What counts as nichush, the forbidden reliance on omens? The Gemara in Chullin 95a examines Rav's ferry, Eliezer's test and Yonasan's sign, with Tosfos.

segulos/praying-on-your-birthday.intro: Some sources treat a birthday as a special time for prayer. The Militzei Eishit writes that it is an auspicious day to ask Hashem for personal requests, citing a pasuk in Tehillim, and Rav Chaim Kanievsky is quoted as suggesting that surgery be scheduled on one's birthday, when mazal is strongest. The discussion grows out of Avodah Zarah 5a and the question of whether birthdays deserve celebration.
segulos/praying-on-your-birthday.description: Is a birthday a favorable time to pray for personal requests? The Militzei Eishit and Rav Chaim Kanievsky on mazal, from the sugya of Avodah Zarah 5a.

segulos/segulah-before-facing-a-judge.intro: Some have a custom to say the name of Avraham Avinu's mother when standing before a judge or an official for a decision. [What’s in a Name?](/daf/bava-basra/91/whats-in-a-name-2024) notes that this segulah is based on the Chida, and the name itself, Amasla'i the daughter of Karnevo, comes from Bava Basra 91a.
segulos/segulah-before-facing-a-judge.description: Why do some say the name of Avraham Avinu's mother before a judge? A segulah based on the Chida, with the name drawn from the Gemara in Bava Basra 91a.

segulos/segulah-for-finding-lost-items.intro: The Steipler would tell people who lost something to recite the Midrash of Rebbe Binyamin: Hagar did not see the well until Hashem opened her eyes. Many combine it with tzedakah for Rebbe Meir Baal Hanes, whose story is told on Avodah Zarah 18. A great-grandson of Rav Aryeh Levine tried both after losing his tefillin, and found them that same morning on a grocery shelf where they had sat for four months.
segulos/segulah-for-finding-lost-items.description: Lost something? The Steipler's advice to read the Midrash of Hagar and the well, combined with tzedakah for Rebbe Meir Baal Hanes from Avodah Zarah 18.

segulos/spilled-wine-as-a-sign-of-blessi.intro: Rebbe Chanin bar Papa said that a house without wine spilled like water is not among the blessed. What does that mean? In Eruvin 65a, Rashi and the Maharsha see it as a measure of wealth, the Meiri reads it as generosity to the poor, the Ben Yehoyada as drinking in moderation, and the Rema as a good omen in itself.
segulos/spilled-wine-as-a-sign-of-blessi.description: What does it mean that a house where wine flows like water is blessed? Rashi, the Maharsha, the Meiri and others explain the Gemara in Eruvin 65a.

angels-and-sheidim/angels-in-the-purim-s.intro: Megillah 15b says three angels were sent so that Achashverosh would agree to speak with Esther, one of them to give her irresistible charm. Later, angels disguised as men uprooted the king's trees and said Haman had ordered it. Even then, an angel had to push Haman onto Esther's couch before the king agreed to hang him, showing how many hidden miracles the salvation needed.
